      "old_english": "**Qūnawī:** Know that no existent described as absolute lacks an aspect toward restriction, even if only through becoming a determinate object of the thought of some thinker or several thinkers. Nor is there any existent judged to be restricted that lacks an aspect toward absoluteness. Yet none knows this except one who knows things completely, after knowing the Real and everything by which the Real is known. Whoever has not tasted this vision has not realized true knowledge of either God or creation.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Every existent describable as absolute has, without exception, some aspect toward restriction: either it already bears a determination or can bear one without being confined to it. This is the respect in which God and creation, and creatures among themselves, stand in relation to one another. The least restriction is that the absolute becomes distinguished as an object in someone's understanding. The conception of a thing requires that it be represented through a likeness by which it is distinguished from other things, whether essentially or accidentally, even at the level of a single instance. Thus the absolute is restricted in an individual's conception without ceasing to be absolute in itself; and in the conceptions of many thinkers it receives representations that are numerically distinct, especially where those representations differ from one mind to another.\n\nEqually, anything judged to be restricted has an aspect toward absoluteness. One cannot make a judgment about the absolute without recognizing some character under which to judge it; once recognized, the character may form the apparent limitation. Yet it still has an aspect toward the absolute, because a limiting predicate inheres in something more fundamental than that predicate, to which thought can return. The bearer cannot simply be eliminated while the predicate remains, for an attribute cannot subsist without a subject. Hence the existence in every conditioned existent is the absolute, intrinsically necessary existence of the Real, which is qualified by the attributes of its loci of appearance.\n\nSuch a point can be understood only by someone who has fully known that things, considered as quiddities, do not themselves possess existence, but are encountered with existence so that it appears through the mirrors they afford and their descriptions become the qualifications of its manifestation. Nonexistent quiddities are not independently attributes of existence, for this would make what exists bear as an intrinsic attribute its contrary, nonexistence; neither are such quiddities the independently existing bearers of existence. Rather, absolute existence is the bearer, and its apparent qualifications arise through its relation to these quiddities.",
      "new_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** ...absoluteness, predominates, so multiplicity does not appear there, although it has an aspect toward finitude with which it is united. Restriction also has an aspect toward absoluteness, but this does not predominate in it and therefore does not appear there; multiplicity appears instead because it is actual there. To the extent that unity appears within restriction, absoluteness is known, though not as the Absolute knows it.\n\n**Qūnawī:** Know that no existent described as absolute lacks an aspect toward restriction, even if only through becoming a determinate object of the thought of some thinker or several thinkers. Nor is there any existent judged to be restricted that lacks an aspect toward absoluteness. Yet none knows this except one who knows things completely, after knowing the Real and knowing everything one knows through Him. Whoever has not tasted this vision has not realized true knowledge of either God or creation.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Every existent describable as absolute has, without exception, some aspect toward restriction: either it already bears a determination or can bear one without being confined to it. This is the respect in which the Real is united with creation, creation with the Real, and some creatures with others. The least restriction is that the absolute becomes distinguished as an object in someone's understanding. The conception of a thing requires that it be represented through a likeness by which it is distinguished from other things, whether essentially or accidentally, even at the level of a single instance. Thus the absolute is restricted in an individual's conception without ceasing to be absolute in itself; and in the conceptions of many thinkers it receives representations that are numerically distinct, especially where those representations differ from one mind to another.\n\nEqually, anything judged to be restricted has an aspect toward absoluteness. One cannot make a judgment about the absolute without recognizing some character under which to judge it; once recognized, the character may form the apparent limitation. Yet it still has an aspect toward the absolute, because a limiting predicate inheres in something more fundamental than that predicate, to which thought can return. The bearer cannot simply be eliminated while the predicate remains, for an attribute cannot subsist without a subject. Hence the existence in every conditioned existent is the absolute, intrinsically necessary existence of the Real, which is qualified by the attributes of its loci of appearance.\n\nSuch a point can be understood only by someone who has fully known that things, considered as quiddities, do not themselves possess existence, but are encountered with existence so that it appears through the mirrors they afford and their descriptions become the qualifications of its manifestation. Nonexistent quiddities are not independently attributes of existence, for this would make what exists bear as an intrinsic attribute its contrary, nonexistence; neither are such quiddities the independently existing bearers of existence. Rather, absolute existence is the bearer, and its apparent qualifications arise through its relation to these quiddities.",

      "old_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing Text Fourteen):** Those qualifications become manifest at the level of relation after having been undifferentiated within the absolute Essence. Their proper understanding requires knowing that the Real is absolute existence, which in turn requires knowing that He exists of Himself: He is necessary, incapable of receiving nonexistence or being transformed into it. Nor is He a mere rational concept without external reality; everything is realized through Him, whereas His reality is through Himself. There is no independent existence belonging to any other.\n\nWhoever has not witnessed this station—that existence is absolute, that it appears under qualifications by relation to its loci, and that the quiddities have no being of their own—has not realized what it means to know the Real as absolute existence. The Real is not an accident inhering in quiddities, nor a thing whose being is conditioned by them; thus He is not multiplied or individually determined by their multiplicity. Nor do creatures possess existence by themselves: they exist through Him, and so remain, considered in themselves, upon the station of nonexistence. The Real, as He always was, has nothing independently coexistent with Him in eternity. Understand.\n\n**[Opening of Text Fifteen, on the same printed page.]**\n\n**Qūnawī (title):** A text explaining the secret of perfection and *greater perfection*.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The preceding text, in saying that every absolute has an aspect toward qualification, might prompt two mistaken thoughts. First, that qualification detracts from the absolute by excluding other qualifications; second, that it makes the absolute more perfect because it previously lacked that qualification. The present text addresses the first mistake by clarifying the secret of perfection and the second by clarifying the secret of the more perfect, after stating a governing distinction.\n\n**Qūnawī:** The Real has an intrinsic perfection and a perfection of the divine names whose manifestation depends on bringing the world into being. Viewed in the light of determination, both are perfections of the names; for every judgment made by a judge concerning something presupposes that the thing judged has become determinate in the judge's conception. Were the Essence not conceived before the names were predicated of it, and distinguished from everything else through its independence in possessing existence, one could not judge it to possess intrinsic perfection. Every determination through which the Real is conceived is one of His names, since among the realizers the names are nothing but determinations of the Real. Hence every perfection predicated of the Real may, under this consideration, be called a perfection of the names. Conversely, insofar as the emanation of the divine names from the presence of His unity is an entailment of His Essence, all the perfections predicated of Him are intrinsic.",
      "new_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing Text Fourteen):** Those qualifications become manifest at the level of relation after having been undifferentiated within the absolute Essence.       "page": 159,
      "entry_id": "MSH-P159",
      "old_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The perfection inseparable from the Real may be considered in three ways. In the first, it is divided into intrinsic and nominal perfection. Intrinsic perfection is that whose existence and manifestation depend on nothing: it is eternally and perpetually manifest to the Essence in the Essence, without dependence on determinations or restrictions, for the Real is independent of all worlds. The existence of nominal perfection, on the other hand, likewise depends on nothing, but its manifestation and actual expression depend on the world's coming to exist, because the names express relations between Essence and things and a relation is not manifested without its terms. This does not mean that the Essence gains a perfection it lacked; rather, after its perfect manifestation to itself, it manifests within distinct loci.\n\nUnder a second consideration, both are perfections of the names: to judge that the Real possesses perfection, one must first conceive what is being judged. Such a conception distinguishes the subject from what lies outside it, however slightly—even, for example, through our conceiving it before the names are attributed to it or through our distinguishing its independence in the possession of existence. Anything distinguished in relation to something else is in that respect determined. Every determination through which the Real is conceived is called a divine name among the realizers, for names are, considered as bare relations, non-existent in themselves and cannot be independent causes of existence. They are in truth determinations of the Real under such relations. Thus there is no predication of perfection without some determination, and both modes of perfection may be called nominal, even when their manifestation does not depend on bringing anything else into existence.\n\nUnder a third consideration, both perfections are intrinsic. Those called intrinsic under the first consideration are plainly so. The others also spring from the presence of divine unity. Unity gives rise to the perspectives of oneness and all-encompassing unity, and the names proceed from the latter. What arises from something which itself arises from the Essence ultimately arises from the Essence. Moreover, its being made manifest is already included in what the Essence entails, for the names are enfolded within it. Hence all the perfections ascribed to the Real may be ascribed to His Essence under this consideration. Understand.\n\n**Qūnawī:** When this has been settled, we say that one whose perfection is from his own Essence cannot be diminished in that perfection by outward accidents and concomitant features in certain levels of manifestation—as though these could undermine it.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This addresses the first apparent difficulty. Perfection that belongs to a thing essentially is its perfection eternally. It is not impaired when, relative to a level or a manifesting locus, it is accompanied by contingent and passing restrictions or by externally associated, more persistent concomitants. Even when those qualifications exclude other or opposite qualifications, they cannot damage intrinsic perfection ... [continued p. 160].",
      "new_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** ...depend on anything, its manifestation and actual realization depend on bringing the world into existence, because the names are relations between the Essence and things, and a relation is realized only through both of its terms.       "entry_id": "MSH-P160",
      "old_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continued):** ...because an attribute attaches to the Real under the consideration of a particular level, not at every other level. He thus remains absolute and, as absolute, perfect. In the first distinction, which separates intrinsic from nominal perfection, the Essence is not altered as names vary any more than it is multiplied by their multiplicity. A particular name's absence at a given level entails no deficiency in the absolute Essence. In the second account, where all perfections are regarded as nominal, every perfection remains in the first determination even if it is not manifest in later determinations; what is absent in one rank is not thereby absent from another. In the third, where all are intrinsic, the Essence is the source of every rank: the source of the first is thereby the source of what proceeds from it, and ultimately the source of all perfections. Understand.\n\n**Qūnawī:** Nor is it permissible to imagine that its perfection contains a deficiency that is then made good by such attributes. Rather, in certain levels, external accidents and concomitants can make apparent the quality of its *greater perfection*; knowledge that this is its manner is itself among those excellences.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This resolves the second difficulty. Essential perfection remains as it always was, while a description of greater perfection becomes manifest, by means of qualifications and concomitants, at levels such as that of the Perfect Human, where divine names appear. This follows readily if intrinsic and nominal perfections are distinguished. If all perfections are called nominal, the perfection belonging to the first determination is unchanged; the additional description of greater perfection belongs to further determinations. And if all are called intrinsic, what belongs to the Essence without mediation remains unchanged, while there is an additional manifestation through intermediaries.\n\nAn objection might arise: does this not, after all, make the Essence complete itself through these manifestations? What is added is only the relation of their appearing in manifesting loci, and a relation, as such, is not another independently existing perfection.       "old_english": "**[Text Sixteen, after the introduction translated on p. 160.]**\n\n**Qūnawī:** The reality of the Real consists of the form of His knowledge of Himself, inasmuch as that knowledge is determined through its relation to Himself, under the consideration in which knowledge, the knower and the known are one.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** What essentially distinguishes the Real from everything else is the form of His knowledge of Himself. Were such a form hypothetically distinct from what it represents, it would correspond perfectly to it. Here, however, the point is the necessary self-relation of knowledge entailed by His conception of Himself. This excludes consideration of God's self-knowledge through His appearance in the loci of manifestation, or through the conception other knowers possess of Him. Nor does His knowledge of Himself involve an added intelligible image standing over against a separately existing subject, with another relation joining them. Such an image would veil the known, and God is exalted above this. It would also introduce multiplicity into the first determination, which is simple from every point of view. Rather, knowing, knower and known are one, because neither the image nor its relation adds something to what is imaged. This excludes the differentiated self-knowledge ascribed under the degree of the names.\n\n**Qūnawī:** His intrinsic attribute, which is not other than His Essence, is a unicity of comprehensiveness—an all-gathering oneness beyond which no gathering, relation or consideration can be conceived.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Qūnawī mentions the intrinsic attribute because it is through such an attribute that the Essence is known to the highest degree available to the knower. It is not other than the Essence in what it refers to, even if the concepts of subject and attribute differ. Without conceptual difference there could be no meaningful predication of an attribute of a subject. The intrinsic attribute is the unique comprehension of existence and all its ranks and descriptions. Nothing more comprehensive can be conceived, for it comprehends both unity as distinguished from differentiation and unity as gathering differentiation, without either opposing the other or restricting the comprehensiveness to one side. There is no special relation confining it to gathering rather than differentiation, nor an unqualified absoluteness superadded to it as a further consideration. It comprehends both the unrestricted and the conditioned without being confined by the very description of comprehending them.\n\n**Qūnawī:** Actual realization of this attribute through witnessing, and complete knowledge of it, consist in knowing that in every determinate thing the Real may be judged determinate according to what makes Him apprehensible in it under determination, while also knowing that He is not confined by that determination and that, considered as He is in Himself, He is undetermined.",
      "new_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The text is noble because it comprehends all the realities described by perfection, and exceedingly noble because it imparts complete knowledge of the subjects and their attributes.\n\n**Qūnawī:** The reality of the Real consists of the form of His knowledge of Himself, inasmuch as that knowledge is determined through its relation to Himself, under the consideration in which knowledge, the knower and the known are one.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** What essentially distinguishes the Real from everything else is the form of His knowledge of Himself.     {
      "page": 162,
      "entry_id": "MSH-P162",
      "old_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī:** To witness this attribute truly, so that one's seeing amounts to the eye or reality of certainty, and to know it completely with the certainty of knowledge, is to recognize the Real in every thing determined as a rank, a branch, or an individual. One may judge the Real determinate in that thing, not because His Essence is intrinsically limited, but because the senses or intellect, or His self-disclosure under names proper to the rank, make Him apprehensible there in a particular manner. The witness must know that He is not restricted by determination at all, much less by the particular determination presently encountered; considered in Himself He is not determined. His appearing in different forms depends on ranks. He therefore retains the purity of His absoluteness while appearing in a determinate locus. To know this is to know an all-embracing unity beyond which no other union, relation or consideration can be placed. Since the attribute had been declared identical in reality with the Essence, Qūnawī now explains this identification.\n\n**Qūnawī:** This is the form of His knowledge of Himself. Thus He knows His Essence as determinate relative to His manifestation in things according to those things, and relative to one who witnesses Him only in a locus; yet He also knows, exalted is He, that considered in Himself He is undetermined, even at the very moment when He is judged determinate, because the apprehension of one who perceives Him only through a locus is limited—whether that locus is regarded as the very reality appearing or as other than it.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** God's being present in each determinate thing in a way that warrants judgment about His appearance there—while not being confined to it and while remaining undetermined in Himself—is what the form of divine self-knowledge signifies. If such a form were an addition, it would perfectly correspond to His reality. In divine self-knowledge the Essence is understood as determinate relative to its appearances in the determinate things, in proportion to their receptive aptitudes, without thereby becoming confined by them. It is also known in relation to the one who sees it only in a locus. Such a person's knowledge is a shadowed participation in divine knowledge as it relates to that person's fixed entity. But God knows, under another consideration not restricted to this relational knowledge, that He is Himself undetermined, even when a creature judges Him determined. This further consideration is not the very same as God's knowing Himself in connection with that limited knower, because a knowledge of something follows what its object is; only the creature perceiving Him under a particular limitation knows Him through that limitation alone. And this holds whether that person takes the locus to be identical with what appears or regards it as something other than what appears ... [continued on p. 163].",
      "new_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī:** To witness this attribute truly, so that one's seeing amounts to the eye or reality of certainty, and to know it completely with the certainty of knowledge, is to recognize the Real in every thing determined as a rank, a branch, or an individual. To know this is to know an all-embracing unity beyond which no other union, relation or consideration can be placed. Since the attribute had been declared identical in reality with the Essence, Qūnawī now explains this identification.\n\n**Qūnawī:** This is the form of His knowledge of Himself. Thus He knows His Essence as determinate relative to His manifestation in things according to those things, and relative to one who witnesses Him only in a locus; yet He also knows, exalted is He, that considered in Himself He is undetermined, even at the very moment when He is judged determinate, because the apprehension of one who perceives Him only through a locus is limited—whether that locus is regarded as the very reality appearing or as other than it.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** God's being present in each determinate thing in a way that warrants judgment about His appearance there—while not being confined to it and while remaining undetermined in Himself—is what the form of divine self-knowledge signifies. If such a form were an addition, it would perfectly correspond to His reality. In divine self-knowledge the Essence is understood as determinate relative to its appearances in the determinate things, in proportion to their receptive aptitudes, without thereby becoming confined by them. It is also known in relation to the one who sees it only in a locus. Such a person's knowledge is a shadowed participation in divine knowledge as it relates to that person's fixed entity. But God knows, under another consideration not restricted to this relational knowledge, that He is Himself undetermined, even when a creature judges Him determined. This further consideration is not the very same as God's knowing Himself in connection with that limited knower, because a knowledge of something follows what its object is; only the creature perceiving Him under a particular limitation knows Him through that limitation alone. This limitation of apprehension applies when the locus is taken as identical with what appears: for example, someone sees God restricted to some manifest things and confines Him there, or instead places Him in all the loci but still confines Him to them. In respect of His knowledge as it relates to these people, He knows Himself ... [continued on p. 163].",

      "old_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continued):** ...In either case the Real knows the person under the aspect of that person's conception of Him, whether the conception is gravely mistaken or true in one respect; and in another aspect He knows Himself as unqualified by that person's conception. Consider this.\n\n**Qūnawī:** The reality of creation consists in the form of their Lord's knowledge of them; their intrinsic quality is *poverty*, which makes manifest absolute richness—but not just any sort of poverty. Understand.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The essential reality distinguishing creatures from the Real, despite the unity of existence, is their form as known in their Lord's knowledge at the second determination. These are the fixed entities (*aʿyān thābita*), not the undifferentiated intrinsic modalities (*shuʾūn*). This is the reality of the fixed entities, not an independently self-subsisting reality of created beings. The intrinsic quality entailed by their nature without mediation is dependence on God: dependence upon Him for the establishment of their intelligible realities in His knowledge, for the existence that appears through them, and for the qualities by which they are known. Such dependence gives expression to the unrestricted self-sufficiency of the Real. The poverty of which Qūnawī speaks is the poverty whose recognition brings to light divine richness; not every species of dependence is the intrinsic quality of creation. For example, the divine names' dependence upon loci for their manifestation is not itself that same creaturely poverty. Understand.\n\n**[Opening of Text Seventeen on the same printed page.] Al-Mahāʾimī:** The following text is called exceedingly noble because the preceding teaching, that the Real's manifestation follows the receptive character of the loci, could suggest He lacks true essential attributes—contrary to reason, transmitted revelation and consensus. The new text therefore examines transcendence or incomparability (*tanzīh*) in its different formulations, identifying what is sound in them. Its nobility lies in joining incomparability and resemblance while affirming every perfection of God without making other things partners with Him, and in declaring Him beyond all descriptions. The resulting insight is deeper than unaided rational understanding or the surface of revealed wording.\n\n**Qūnawī:** The fruit of rational incomparability is to distinguish the Real from what is called other than Him through negative attributes, out of concern for imagined deficiencies that are posited in minds but do not occur in existence.       "page": 164,
      "entry_id": "MSH-P164",
      "old_english": "**[Qūnawī's Qurʾānic illustrations, continued:]** God is described as the best of providers (Qurʾān 62:11), the best of creators (23:14), the most merciful of those who show mercy (7:151), and greater than anything that can be compared with Him (cf. 9:72), and similarly elsewhere.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** God is declared incomparable through reason, revealed law and unveiling, but their modes of incomparability are not the same. Reason exempts Him from certain features because it regards them as deficiencies. By excluding these, reason attributes to Him negative qualifications opposite to them. The rational procedure thus distinguishes the Real from other things by such negations. Qūnawī does not accept this result as sufficient: deficiencies, as deficiencies, are privative considerations and cannot belong to existence in itself. Everything that actually exists has perfection insofar as it exists. Deficiency is posited by the understanding when a manifestation occurs in one locus rather than another. Nor is there contradiction within existence as such; opposition belongs to comparisons between definite ranks.\n\nThe author calls this the *fruit* rather than the true content of rational incomparability, because he does not accept the idea that God's distinction from all other things consists of His possessing attributes that they lack, or their possessing attributes excluded from Him. This would prevent the Real from embracing all perfections and would fail to establish the most complete unity.\n\nAs for the incomparability communicated by the outward sense of Scripture, the expressions of the Book, the Sunna and the public statements of learned authorities exclude a partner, equal or like in the rank of divinity. Its consequence is the denial of several independently existing gods. Qūnawī specifies existential plurality rather than merely conceptual plurality. Yet even this is not the whole matter, for revealed speech also attributes such positive perfections as hearing, seeing, life, knowledge, power, will and speech to creatures, without equating them with divine attributes. The denial of likeness does not abolish attribution of the same general terms under unequal modes. In speaking of God as the *best* of providers and creators, and the most merciful of the merciful, Scripture itself retains a grammatical comparison with other providers and merciful agents. The surface reading, taken to deny all commonality whatsoever, is therefore incomplete; a fuller understanding must reconcile the scriptural expressions. That is the work of the incomparability disclosed through unveiling (*kashf*).\n\n**Qūnawī (opening of the account of unveiled incomparability):** The incomparability understood by the people of unveiling is to affirm the Real's universal comprehensiveness without limiting Him to the description of comprehending; it distinguishes the rulings proper to the various divine names.       "new_english": "**Continuation:** ...[the printed source cites Qurʾān 9:72], and similar expressions.\n\n**Editorial source note:** Q 9:72 says “approval from God is greater”; the source’s short phrase “God is greater” is not a verbatim quotation of that verse.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** God is declared incomparable through reason, revealed law and unveiling, but their modes of incomparability are not the same.       "entry_id": "MSH-P165",
      "old_english": "**Qūnawī:** The same applies to divine attributes. Among the fruits of unveiled incomparability is the denial of any independently existing 'other' while retaining the numerical rulings that distinguish one appearance from another. This involves no positing of a deficiency that must be negated, nor conceiving a perfection that needs to be added to the Real through some further affirmation. Peace.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Here the author states the very principle of incomparability rather than merely its consequence, signalling that this mode of transcendence, unlike the preceding conceptions, is valid from the outset. Under unveiled incomparability, nothing is excluded from the Reality's comprehensiveness; yet that comprehensiveness does not enclose or delimit Him. He is present in differentiation as well as in unity. The Real thus has a unity comprehending both gathering and distinction, taken together and separately. This concerns the Essence.\n\nFor the names, unveiled incomparability means not attributing to one name every ruling that applies to another. Certain rulings cannot belong to a name *qua* that name, even though they belong to another. The Essence comprehends them all: the rulings of the name that abases cannot, *as such*, be assigned to the name that exalts, and vice versa. Qūnawī therefore makes the authentic principle and its fruit explicit. The negation of a separate 'other' follows from comprehensiveness, while the numerical distinction of appearances remains. Were every numerical distinction simply erased, differentiation would have no place and the Real would be confined to pure gathering. Thus what is called other than Him under one consideration is not independent of Him under another.\n\nNor does this imply an original deficiency in the Essence that is overcome by including all things. All their possibilities are comprehended there, so the Essence is not deficient; no new event alters it. Similarly, one cannot suppose that the Real acquires a perfection through some newly affirmed creaturely attribute. The Real is essentially perfect, and the perfections displayed under restriction belong in reality to Him as the ground of their manifestation.\n\nThe author's concluding expression 'peace' may be read as a salutation of those who practise this unveiled incomparability and avoid the limitation of the earlier viewpoints. Thus the Qurʾānic conclusion is appropriate: 'Glory be to your Lord, Lord of might, beyond what they describe' (37:180), for creatures' formulations of incomparability and resemblance do not exhaust Him; 'peace be upon the messengers' (37:181), because of the correctness of the transcendence they convey; and 'praise be to God, Lord of the worlds' (37:182), for He comprehends the whole without diminution or change and all perfections belong to Him.       "page": 166,
      "entry_id": "MSH-P166",
      "old_english": "**Qūnawī:** A noble text.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** In the preceding text it was said that all things subsist in the Real, although the Eternal cannot be the receptive locus of originated events. Earlier, it had been said that the Real pervades all things, although the Eternal is too exalted to be contained in the originated. This noble text removes that apparent difficulty, since it explains how something originated may be described as eternal under one consideration, and how the Eternal may be described as newly appearing under another. The preceding statement, that every absolute reality has an aspect toward determination and vice versa, is not thereby overturned.\n\n**Qūnawī:** The manner in which anything is in something else follows the character of its locus, whether that locus is intelligible or formal. Consequently, the possible objects of knowledge, insofar as their determinations are established and inscribed in the knowledge of the Real, are described as pre-eternal. Likewise, everything determined in divine knowledge bears, under another aspect, the ruling of origination: the existence of the world and the knowledge possessed by its inhabitants are originated and receptive, unlike the existence and knowledge of the Real. Know this, and, if God wills, you will be rightly guided.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The establishment of any state in a locus is qualified as originated or pre-eternal in accordance with the locus, even if considered in itself that state would not be so qualified. This is true whether the locus is intelligible, such as the Creator's knowledge or created intellects, or formal, as in elemental bodies.\n\nThe possible objects of knowledge are originated by their own nature. Nevertheless, they are described as pre-eternal insofar as their determinations subsist in the eternal divine knowledge: what is established in that knowledge as an object of knowledge is not something temporally superadded to it. One must not make divine knowledge a place in which new events come to be. The same determined objects, which are described as eternal insofar as they are known by God, are subject to the ruling of origination insofar as they exist externally. The being of the cosmos and the knowledge of its inhabitants are originated in their outward existence, for they are receptive of and dependent on God's existence and knowledge.\n\nThis is not the case with the existence and knowledge of the Real, which are eternal considered in themselves. When originated things appear, the ancient existence and knowledge may be described as newly appearing **with respect to manifestation and relation**, not through an origination in themselves. The Eternal is related to the originated and thus receives a relative description without changing in His own reality. Understand this and you will reconcile the outward law (*sharīʿa*) and the inner reality (*ḥaqīqa*) at the point from which pure divine unity proceeds, if God wills.",

      "page": 167,
      "entry_id": "MSH-P167",
      "old_english": "**Qūnawī:** A noble text, among the noblest, most majestic and most comprehensive statements of the universal principles of divine and cosmic knowledge.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The preceding text examined a thing under the aspect of the locus in which it is established; the present text considers what belongs to it under the aspect of itself. It discusses the divine realities: the Essence, its essential names and their rulings, its essential efficacy and being effective, its knowledge and its unity; the way its knowledge acts as a mirror of the Essence and names and as the source of multiplicity; and the ranks, their relations and the arising of some from others. The text is noble because it gathers the results of the previous texts, majestic because it includes their premises, and comprehensive because it unites beginnings and ends.\n\n**Qūnawī:** Know that the application of the name *Essence* (*dhāt*) is true of the Real only in respect of His determination: that first determination which, in the conception of creatures other than the perfected, comes after an imagined absoluteness whose nature is unknown and which has no name. That supposed absoluteness is a negative description of the Essence, imagined as distinct from every determination. The affirmative reality actually given, however, is the first determination.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Beginners in this discipline sometimes suppose that the name *Essence* belongs to the Real under the aspect of sheer absoluteness. But this absoluteness is a negative meaning, without a known attribute or a name. They call it the unseen of the Real because, according to their supposition, it stands above everything. If *Essence* named something below this absoluteness, the absoluteness would be above the divine Essence; yet all agree that nothing is above Him.\n\nThe supposition derives from the reasoning that every determination is preceded by non-determination, and that non-determination is absoluteness. Qūnawī corrects it. The word *Essence* signifies the Real under consideration of the first determination, since there is, by agreement, no name preceding it. To make *Essence* the name of something prior to that determination contradicts the very assertion that the supposed prior absoluteness is not circumscribed by being an essence, just as it is not circumscribed by any description. Moreover, the Real's intelligible determination in His knowledge of Himself is considered at the first determination: what has not been conceived under that aspect by the Real cannot be conceived as something superordinate by another knower, so that the name *Essence* could be applied to it.\n\nWhat the unperfected understand as a prior absoluteness is thus a mental supposition formed by contrast with various modes of absoluteness and restriction. It is a negative description, not another entity higher than the Real. Something can stand above another only if it is itself something. If one objects that it must be something because it is distinguished from all determination, the answer is that the distinction is imposed by imagination; it places an imagined non-determination above every real determination. [The argument continues on p. 168.]",

      "old_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** Non-determination is a negative consideration and therefore cannot genuinely be above or prior to what is determined. The first determination alone is the affirmative reality at issue. Accordingly, *the divine Essence* is a name applied there, not a name for a non-existent abstraction. Certainly one may describe the Essence negatively as not confined by either absoluteness or restriction. That is an account relative to the ranks, not an additional state prior to the first determination. Because it commonly figures in ordinary people's conception, they imagine it to precede that first determination. Understand.\n\n**Qūnawī:** The Essence intrinsically comprehends the essential names, the keys of the unseen; and the referent of the name *Essence* is in no respect other than its names. The names, however, differ from and oppose one another; and again they are united with one another from the standpoint of the Essence that comprehends them all.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The first determination intrinsically includes the essential names, the keys of the unseen and of the divine relations: the Living, the Knowing, the Powerful, the Willing, the Hearing, the Seeing and the Speaking. Were these names present only through a further intermediary, that intermediary, rather than the essential names themselves, would be the key of the unseen.\n\nAn objection might be raised: if the first determination included several names, it would no longer be the first determination but already the presence of the names. The answer is that in the first presence the One named by the term *Essence* differs in no respect from His names. In their own presence, the second determination, the names differ conceptually from one another, sometimes oppose one another in their rulings, and also agree in the comprehending Essence. Thus they may be predicated of one another in one respect and all of them predicated of the Essence. Unity at the first determination is not equivalent to the abolition of the names; nor is their differentiation at the second equivalent to a plurality of independent essences.\n\n**Qūnawī:** Unicity (*aḥadiyya*) describes the determination, not an absolutely unqualified something supposed to be determined, since what is absolutely unqualified has no name and no attribute.\n\n*Editorial note:* An explanatory footnote to *aḥadiyya* is present in the online transcription but is not represented here as part of Qūnawī's or al-Mahāʾimī's running medieval text. The argument continues on p. 169.",

The names, however, differ from and oppose one another; and again they are united with one another from the standpoint of the Essence that comprehends them all.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The first determination intrinsically includes the essential names, the keys of the unseen and of the divine relations: the Living, the Knowing, the Powerful, the Willing, the Hearing, the Seeing and the Speaking. Were these names present only through a further intermediary, that intermediary, rather than the essential names themselves, would be the key of the unseen.\n\nAn objection might be raised: if the first determination included several names, it would no longer be the first determination but already the presence of the names.       "old_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This anticipates an objection. How can the Essence include the essential realities expressed by the names if it is called *Essence* at its first determination, when only the Essence alone can be conceived? Is it not called unicity precisely because the names are not distinguished there? How, then, can it comprehend them under that aspect?\n\nQūnawī's reply is that absolute indetermination, as such, does not become determined and has neither name nor attribute. Hence it cannot itself be described as determination or unicity. In the consideration of *aḥadiyya* the names are not distinguished; in that of *wāḥidiyya* the names are taken into account. Yet the Essence is more comprehensive than the descriptions of it as either unicity or unitive plurality, and can therefore comprehend the names without their becoming separately distinguished in the first consideration. Understand.\n\n**Qūnawī:** From the standpoint of these names, insofar as the Essence does not differ from them, we say that the Real acts by the Essence. Understand.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This follows from the names' non-otherness in relation to the Essence. The realized knowers can therefore say that the Essence effects things without an intermediary. On the other hand, the Essence considered solely in itself is self-sufficient beyond the worlds, so the operation of the names must also be acknowledged. Yet those names are the very Essence at the rank of unicity, and are included by the Essence at the rank of *wāḥidiyya*. Under the former respect and in their actual referent, what appears to be an intermediary is not a second entity standing between the Essence and its effect. Qūnawī's injunction to understand indicates that those who speak of an intermediary also speak truly, but under a different consideration.\n\n**Qūnawī:** The Essence has just one inseparable concomitant, different from it only relationally; that concomitant is knowledge.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Consider the seven essential names. The Essence has one first concomitant, whether approached under the aspect of *aḥadiyya* or of *wāḥidiyya*; the others follow through it, in the order of intelligible dependence. Even this first concomitant is not really separate from the Essence. Under the differentiated aspect of *wāḥidiyya* it is distinct only by relation, and under unicity the knower, knowledge and known are united from every aspect. Thus what might be spoken of as an intermediary between Essence and the other essential names is not an intermediary in any fully independent sense.\n\nQūnawī specifies *knowledge*, rather than *life*, as the immediate concomitant.       "old_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** All these essential attributes are eternal and everlasting.       "old_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** When one says that knowledge is the mirror of the Essence, the operative term is *like* a mirror. It would be impossible for a thing to depend on itself as on an independent second thing. What makes the expression legitimate is the relative intelligible distinction between divine knowledge and the Essence at the second consideration, the distinction made possible by considering the Essence's relation of understanding itself. Through that merely conceptual difference the Real's determination in His self-understanding can be conceived. His very Self is like a mirror for His Self, and since His knowledge is His Self, His intrinsic knowledge may all the more appropriately be called His mirror.\n\n**Qūnawī:** For this reason we said elsewhere that the reality of the Real is the form of His knowledge of Himself. Remember.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This recalls the treatment of the Real's self-knowledge earlier in the work. Knowledge may be likened to the mirror of the Essence because its difference is relational and conceptual rather than real. This is the exception to the ordinary rule: where created things are concerned, what appears is distinct from its locus under at least one aspect; in the unique case of the Real the manifest and the locus can be the same Reality. The reader is asked to remember the different earlier discussions in order to understand the exception correctly.\n\n**Qūnawī:** As for the *ranks* (*marātib*), they are universal determinations encompassed by the single intrinsic concomitant, knowledge. They are like loci passed through by the unrestricted effusion issuing from the Essence, considering the non-otherness of the effusion and its giver, as previously noted in connection with the Real's being manifest and being a locus of manifestation.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The ranks are universal determinations, and universals insofar as they are universal have their being in knowledge. Knowledge, the one intrinsic concomitant, therefore comprehends the ranks. They are inscribed therein just as the Essence is mirrored therein, though their two kinds of inscription must not be confused. The ranks have their distinct forms in the presence of knowledge, and in that sense are like the places through which the universal effusion passes. These forms qualify the effusion according to the receptivities of the ranks. [Continued p. 172.]",

      "page": 172,
      "entry_id": "MSH-P172",
      "old_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing from p. 171):** The universal effusion from the Essence, in passing through the intelligible ranks, is delimited by the particular capacities of those ranks. It is called unrestricted because the manifest and the locus of manifestation are united at the first determination, the rank of unity. Here the source of the effusion is the manifest Reality, and the effusion is what constitutes the appearance through its locus; at that level, they are not two independent things. The effusion is qualified only through the additional forms that belong to the ranks as they are inscribed in the divine knowledge.\n\n**Qūnawī:** The ranks have a share in the reality of producing an effect, though not absolutely: they do so insofar as they are, as I have said, like loci.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Since the effusion becomes differentiated as it traverses the ranks, they contribute to its effective determination. The single unrestricted effusion is qualified and multiplied by the differentiated loci; before these considerations there is no such qualification, because effusion and giver are considered one. But the ranks do not exercise efficacy absolutely. As was shown in an earlier text, a thing is an agent in the fullest sense only if it is effective as that very thing, without having to introduce an additional qualification or some external excellence. In the present case, the rank's effect depends precisely on the addition of its function as an intelligible locus. This is a qualified, not absolutely independent, causality.\n\n**Qūnawī:** Every rank is therefore an intelligible place of disclosure for a group of rulings of existence and possibility. Those rulings branch from the essential names, from the principal divine names, and from the derivative names which follow them.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Each rank is an intelligible mirror for the rulings of necessity and possibility, much as a receptacle displays the colour of what it contains: one says that water takes on the colour of its vessel. The rulings of necessity concern effective agency; those of possibility concern receptivity. The two kinds are joined in each rank without being simply identical. The former branch from the essential names that do not signify realities added to the Essence—for instance the names *He*, *God*, *Existence*, *Pre-eternal*, *All-knowing*, and *Manifest*. They also branch from the mothers of the divine names, that is, the primary names previously described as the keys of the unseen. The rulings of possibility branch from the following or derivative names, such as Creator, Provider and Fashioner, in their connections to the receptivities of creatures. It is through the rulings of these names that the ranks have the efficacy being discussed. In ultimate truth the efficacious source is the names, and hence the Essence to which they belong.       "new_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing from p. 171):** The universal effusion from the Essence, in passing through the intelligible ranks, is delimited by the particular capacities of those ranks. This is a qualified, not absolutely independent, causality.\n\n**Qūnawī:** Every rank is therefore an intelligible place of disclosure for a group of rulings of existence and possibility. Those rulings branch from the essential names, from the principal divine names, and from the derivative names which follow them.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Each rank is an intelligible mirror for the rulings of necessity and possibility, just as a sensible locus acts upon what appears within it: “The colour of water is the colour of its vessel.” The rulings of necessity concern effective agency; those of possibility concern receptivity. The two kinds are joined in each rank without being simply identical. The former branch from the essential names that do not signify realities added to the Essence—for instance the names *He*, *God*, *Existence*, *Pre-eternal*, *All-knowing*, and *Manifest*. They also branch from the mothers of the divine names, that is, the primary names previously described as the keys of the unseen. The rulings of possibility branch from the following or derivative names, such as Creator, Provider and Fashioner, in their connections to the receptivities of creatures. It is through the rulings of these names that the ranks have the efficacy being discussed. In ultimate truth the efficacious source is the names, and hence the Essence to which they belong. Understand.\n\n**Qūnawī (opening of the next sentence):** The ranks have fixed entities in the domain of divine knowledge and intelligible apprehension, and ... [continued p. 173].",
      "reasons": [

    {
      "page": 173,
      "entry_id": "MSH-P173",
      "old_english": "**Qūnawī (continuing):** ...they do not exercise an effect independently, but only through existence. Such too is the relation of the rulings of necessity to the ranks: these rulings are effective, and their effects appear in all that is related to a rank and becomes determined there, through the conditioning of unrestricted effusion as it reaches and passes through the rank.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The text explicitly repeats that it is **the ranks**, not the previously mentioned names, that have fixed entities, lest the pronoun be taken as referring to the nearest antecedent. Their mode of efficacy is that of intelligible loci of the combined rulings of necessity and possibility. The fixed entities considered as intelligible forms are, under that respect, non-existent externally; the non-existent does not act upon what exists. The qualified effusion, however, is existential and realized externally. Thus the fixed entities possess no independent power to produce it. Their effect is through existence, which carries the rulings of necessity through the essential names, and the rulings of possibility through the derivative names.\n\nWhy, then, does Qūnawī not simply attribute the entire effect to existence? Because existence as unrestricted does not, by itself and as unqualified, account for the variety of its concrete appearances. Considered in its unity, the effusion is one; its differentiation depends on the ranks. Their rulings appear in every effusion that relates to them. The relation called 'contact' is not a physical collision. It is the effect's becoming determined at a rank, according to that rank's capacity. An effusion that **arrives and remains** at a rank is conditioned in one manner, whereas an effusion **passing through** it toward another rank is conditioned in another manner. These differences account for why ranks may have an effect even when a disclosure is not arrested within them.\n\nNor is it enough to give this efficacy exclusively to the rulings of necessity and possibility. Those rulings do not stand alone; they have to be established under the ranks. The resulting causal account therefore considers the intelligible ranks together with the relevant divine and possible rulings. Understand.\n\n**Qūnawī:** The ranks are like relative endpoints when one considers the course of essential effusion and existential self-disclosure through the stations and degrees determined between eternity without beginning and eternity without end—without a final goal or fixed resting-place.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This answers an objection. If ranks influence effusion only when effusion reaches and is determined at them, how can they condition what merely passes through them? Because each rank is a **relative limit** in relation to a disclosure's course, whether the disclosure remains there or continues through it. The commentary continues on p. 174.",
      "new_english": "**Qūnawī (continuing):** ...they do not exercise an effect independently, but only through existence. Such too is the relation of necessity to the ranks: the ranks are effective, and their ruling is manifest in everything that comes into contact with them and becomes determined with them, through the conditioning of unrestricted effusion as it reaches and passes through the rank.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The text explicitly repeats that it is **the ranks**, not the previously mentioned names, that have fixed entities, lest the pronoun be taken as referring to the nearest antecedent. Their mode of efficacy is that of intelligible loci of the combined rulings of necessity and possibility. The fixed entities considered as intelligible forms are, under that respect, non-existent externally; the non-existent does not act upon what exists. The qualified effusion, however, is existential and realized externally. Thus the fixed entities possess no independent power to produce it. Their effect is through existence, which carries the rulings of necessity through the essential names, and the rulings of possibility through the derivative names.\n\nWhy, then, does Qūnawī not simply attribute the entire effect to existence? Because existence as unrestricted does not, by itself and as unqualified, account for the variety of its concrete appearances. Considered in its unity, the effusion is one; its differentiation depends on the ranks. Their rulings appear in every effusion that relates to them. The relation called 'contact' is not a physical collision. It is the effect's becoming determined at a rank, according to that rank's capacity. An effusion that **arrives and remains** at a rank is conditioned in one manner, whereas an effusion **passing through** it toward another rank is conditioned in another manner. These differences account for why ranks may have an effect even when a disclosure is not arrested within them.\n\nNor is it enough to give this efficacy exclusively to the rulings of necessity and possibility. Those rulings do not stand alone; they have to be established under the ranks. The resulting causal account therefore considers the intelligible ranks together with the relevant divine and possible rulings. Understand.\n\n**Qūnawī:** The ranks are like relative endpoints when one considers the course of essential effusion and existential self-disclosure through the stations and degrees determined between eternity without beginning and eternity without end—without a final goal or fixed resting-place.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This answers an objection. If ranks influence effusion only when effusion reaches and is determined at them, how can they condition what merely passes through them? He says that the ranks are relative endpoints, whether one considers effusion as arriving at them—so that their existence endures from eternity without beginning to eternity without end, as with the sanctified spirits—or as passing through them. Some do not endure, and effusion moves from them to others. Even where the share proper to a rank does not pass from it to another, it passes, through the mediation of effusion ... [continued on p. 174].",

      "old_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** A rank may serve as the relative endpoint for the effusion that sustains its own existence through the whole duration allotted to it, as in the case of sanctified spirits. Or it may be a relative endpoint for an effusion that passes onward to other ranks. Even where the special share proper to that rank does not leave it, the effusion proceeds through it toward things below it in rank and acts upon them. For that reason every rank is a relative destination: at each, what reaches it becomes determinate according to its capacity.\n\nThe ranks are relative endpoints by reference to the journey of essential effusion, that is, existential self-disclosure, through successive stations and degrees. The term *stations* may be applied to those points from which the effusion moves altogether to another place; *degrees* to the remaining differences of order, including those in which a disclosure endures while another proceeds. The series is situated between what is without beginning and what is without end, yet there is no last goal beyond which nothing remains, and no absolute cessation at the point already reached. New creation (*khalq jadīd*) is constantly realized across the instances of manifestation. Movement is treated here as an affirmative existential event, whereas rest, insofar as it is the sheer negation of movement, is privative. Consequently the course of disclosure is ceaseless. A rank thus counts as the end of what has preceded it, but not as the absolute end of what succeeds it. Understand.\n\n**Qūnawī:** It is now evident from what I have explained that the ranks gather the groups of rulings that stand established within them from the presences of necessity and possibility. They make manifest the results of their conjunction, but according to the ranks themselves—not simply according to the rulings taken alone, nor according to unrestricted effusion alone. Their relation is that of shapes and moulds to things shaped and moulded when these reach and occupy them. This is their efficacy. They are fixed in their intelligible entities; the resulting rulings are traced back to them and ultimately attributed to them, for they are their source and their return. Understand.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** A rank gathers the rulings of necessity and possibility that apply to it, and these remain established relative to it, even if a particular effusion passes away from it or affects something else through it. The rulings arise from the divine and necessary names and from the names connected with the possible realm, whose respective presences abide. Accordingly the rulings derived from them also have a stable intelligible place.\n\nThe ranks manifest the results produced by the conjunction of the two orders of rulings. The manifestation is ascribed to the rank as the intelligible mirror and place of conjunction, not to the rulings taken in abstraction: without their place of establishment they are not independent agents. Nor can it be attributed merely to unrestricted effusion, which, as such, does not independently produce its own differentiation. This is clarified by comparing a rank with a shape or mould: the arriving effusion receives a determinate form, while the mould, under the relevant consideration, stays as it is.       "old_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The fixed entities of the ranks remain established in the domain of knowledge. The results of the assembled rulings are referred to them, since the effects are the effects of those intelligible realities; the difference of outcomes follows from the difference of the fixed entities. Consequently the variation of recompense is connected with the determinate recipients and their acts, not with a wholly undifferentiated divine command considered in isolation. These determinate entities are the sites where recompense occurs, while necessity and its rulings do not, by themselves, become recipients of reward or punishment. The ranks are also the points from which the relevant actions proceed. The Qurʾānic expression 'as a recompense for what they used to do' states this relationship. None of this implies that the fixed entities have existence independently of God; their existence is through Him and His self-disclosure. Understand: the point enables the joining of divine determination (*qadar*) and revealed obligation (*sharʿ*).\n\n**Qūnawī:** Then know that the ranks are linked by the emergence of some from others, and the names are likewise ordered. Divinity, together with its universal names—the Living, the Knowing, the Powerful and the Willing—is a shadow of the Essence insofar as the Essence intrinsically comprises the keys of the unseen. Yet between divinity and the Essence under that aspect there is a subtle difference, disclosed to the perfected in their direct experience. In the divine presence the degree of divinity is conceived as distinct from the principal names just mentioned. The Essence, however, is conceived as different from its essential names only by those veiled from essential self-disclosure. Those to whom essential self-disclosure is granted neither conceive nor witness that kind of separation, except when they consider their knowledge of how the veiled conceive it. Their true distinction follows what I have indicated: the Essence is in no respect other than its essential names, although the names differ among themselves and cannot be separated from the Essence. And the degrees of the keys of the unseen are unequal, some following others; the same has been shown of the derivative divine names, such as Creator, Originator and Fashioner. Remember.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The earlier account treated each rank as a relative terminus; this passage shows that the ranks also have an order in which one proceeds from another, following the corresponding order of the names. The presence of divinity is *wāḥidiyya*, with the four principal names just mentioned. These four are called universal because the Hearing and Seeing are comprehended under the Knowing, while the Speaking is referred to the Powerful and the Willing. Divinity in that respect is the shadow of the Essence in its *aḥadiyya*, in which the seven essential names are gathered as the keys of the unseen.\n\nYet if *aḥadiyya* contains the same essential names as *wāḥidiyya*, why are they two ranks? The difference is precise and is understood according to the mode in which names are distinctly conceived and actually manifest.       "old_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** In the rank of divinity the names are manifested in actual differentiation; in the rank of unicity they are not conceived as different from the Essence, because their distinguishing appearances are still gathered in it without being separated. Those veiled from this truth speak as though there were no names and attributes at all at the level of the Essence and as though all names belonged exclusively to the divine presence. Some accordingly deny the possibility of essential self-disclosure: they imagine the Essence as stripped of all attributes and therefore unable to disclose itself, given its independence of the worlds; yet self-disclosure necessarily has the meaning of being manifest.\n\nThose to whom the Essence is disclosed do not conceive the distinction as one between an attribute-less Essence and a presence in which attributes first come to exist. They do not witness such a distinction in essential disclosure. For to disclose itself is to be manifest, and in this perspective the disclosure of the Essence entails the manifestation of all things, since the Real is what appears in everything while also remaining inwardly hidden from all. They can nevertheless understand the distinction when they consider the understanding of those who are veiled. The reader should recall that passage to integrate the ranks, essential names, derivative names and the modes in which each produces its effect. Understand.",
      "new_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** In the rank of divinity the names are manifested in actual differentiation; in the rank of unicity they are not conceived as different from the Essence, because they are there potentially. In the chapter explaining the remaining secrets of Text Eleven he said, “The names are states ...” Understand.\n\n### Text Twenty\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Since the arising of some ranks from others requires an affinity connecting what comes after to what precedes, he says:\n\n**Qūnawī:** A chapter on connection.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** That is, on the connection of some names with others, whereby some arise from others and are ordered after them.\n\n**Qūnawī:** The secret of affinities lies in sharing that which removes the rulings of otherness under the aspect that establishes the affinity.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** That is, the cause of affinity and the animating principle that sustains ...       "page": 177,
      "entry_id": "MSH-P177",
      "old_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī:** If some ranks arise from others, there must be a fitting relationship between what precedes and what follows, such that the subsequent rank is connected with its predecessor.\n\n**Qūnawī:** A chapter on connection.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** That is, on the connection of certain divine names with others, whereby some arise from and are ordered after others.\n\n**Qūnawī:** The secret of affinities (*munāsabāt*) lies in sharing something that removes the rulings of mutual otherness under the aspect in which affinity is established.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The reason that two things can be suitably related is that they share an aspect in virtue of which the differentiation between them is set aside—though in another respect they remain different, so that one can precede the other and the other follow it. Affinity (*munāsaba*) may be **intrinsic** (*dhātiyya*) or a matter of **rank** (*martabiyya*). Intrinsic affinity occurs between the Real and the human being, or between human individuals; rank-based affinity is here treated among human individuals. The two kinds must not be confused.\n\n**Qūnawī:** The first and highest is intrinsic affinity. Between the Real and the human being—who is the intended locus—it is established in two ways. The first concerns the weakness of the effect of the human being as a mirror upon the self-disclosure determined in that mirror, so that it does not give the disclosure a qualification incompatible with divine transcendence, beyond the necessary qualification of determination. That qualification does not impugn the greatness, majesty and oneness of the Real. This also involves freedom from most of the rulings of possibility and from the properties of intervening mediations. The different degrees of the ones brought near and of the solitary perfected ones derive from this aspect.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Intrinsic affinity comes first because it concerns the highest and earliest ranks of manifestation. Among loci it belongs in the fullest sense to the human being, and especially to the perfect human, who is the intended end of manifestation. One aspect of this affinity is negative or privative: the mirror's own fixed reality exerts the least possible limitation on the self-disclosure that appears within it. The less the mirror's individual properties distort the disclosure, the more closely the appearance resembles its source under the aspect of transcendence. Yet a created mirror cannot be altogether without an effect, for what appears in it necessarily has the determination of appearing in *this* mirror rather than another.\n\nUnder strict comparison, even that determination is less than the unrestricted Reality. The image is a shadow and cannot equal that whose shadow it is; a determinate shadow cannot encompass the majesty of its source; and determination as distinct from its source implies a relative duality. The difficulty is only resolved when determinate manifestation is not confused with the Essence considered in itself. The same negative affinity comes from the high rank's relative freedom from possible limitations and from intermediary properties. Proximity to the Real means that the rulings of necessity are more evident and the limitations of possibility less evident in the manifestation. [Continued p. 178.]",

      "old_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** When the rulings of necessity predominate, intrinsic affinity is established under the first aspect.\n\n**Qūnawī:** The differences in degree of the ones brought near—the poles and solitary individuals—before the Real follow from this aspect.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** One whose mirror has the weaker limiting effect, and whose rank is less burdened by the rulings of possibility, enjoys greater proximity; the contrary condition entails a lesser degree of proximity.\n\n**Qūnawī:** The second aspect of affinity with the Real is according to the servant's share in the form of the divine presence. This share varies with the measure of comprehensive gathering (*jamʿiyya*) in the person. Affinity strengthens or weakens with the narrowness or breadth of the circle of the human being's comprehensiveness, in accordance with the receptivity of that person: one has fewer shares where that circle is restricted, and more where it is expanded.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The second aspect is affirmative: the servant's acquiring the moral qualities and displaying attributes that reflect the divine names, in a way appropriate to created existence. In virtue of his reality as the **isthmus of isthmuses** (*barzakh al-barāzikh*), he mirrors both the Essence and divinity together with their concomitants. Affinity strengthens or weakens with the narrowness or breadth of the circle of the human being's comprehensiveness, in accordance with the receptivity of that person: one has fewer shares where that circle is restricted, and more where it is expanded.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The second aspect is affirmative: the servant's acquiring the moral qualities and displaying attributes that reflect the divine names, in a way appropriate to created existence. It does **not** mean that a divine attribute migrates from God to the servant, or that numerically the same attribute inheres in two subjects. Rather, the servant receives a share in a spiritual and intelligible *image* of the divine presence, not a material image and not an independent share in the divine Essence. The broader the servant's comprehension of the moral qualities and attributes through which divine names are manifested, the stronger the affinity. The breadth or narrowness of that gathering follows the person's fixed entity as a mirror, its aptitude and receptivity. Consequently the same disclosure is received in unequal degrees.\n\n**Qūnawī:** One who comprehends the attributes and rulings included in necessity and possibility, insofar as they can actually be manifested in any age, and who also possesses affinity under the first aspect, is the one who has perfection. That person is loved by the Real and is intended for his own sake. In virtue of his reality as the **isthmus of isthmuses** (*barzakh al-barāzikh*), he mirrors both the Essence and divinity together with their concomitants. One possessing the first aspect alone is beloved and brought near, but is not the intended end in that same complete sense.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Since at least one of the two aspects must obtain, the two can also be combined. Thus the one who gathers what the station of necessity comprises of divine attributes, and what the station of possibility comprises of the rulings of the ranks, on condition that it is possible ... [continued on p. 179].",

      "old_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The perfected individual exhibits the first affinity, because the mirror's conditioning action is slight and the limitations of possibility are diminished. He also gathers the second affinity, because the possible manifestations of divine attributes and of the cosmic ranks are comprehended in him. Other isthmuses mediate necessity and possibility or spirits and bodies. The complete human reality, however, is a mirror of the Essence insofar as it comprehends the intrinsic names without otherness and a mirror of the divine presence insofar as it comprehends the names and their consequences among necessity and possibility. For the determinations of human spirits from the spiritual worlds and their unequal nobility and spiritual dignity are connected with the number and strength of the mediations between them and the first principle, and with the multiplicity or weakness of possible limitations. After God's decree and determination, the decisive condition in this ordering is temperament, in accordance with which a spirit becomes individually determined. The temperament closer to genuine equilibrium, the centre around which the perfected souls are determined ... [continued p. 180].",
      "new_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** ...for those attributes and rulings to appear in actuality in every age and time.       "old_english": "**Qūnawī (continuing):** ...receives a more noble and elevated spirit in relation to the ranks of the higher intellects and souls. A temperament further from the point of equilibrium receives what corresponds to a lower rank and a lesser measure of nobility.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Intrinsic affinity between human beings has two aspects analogous to the divine–human case. The first is a relative absence of dissimilarity in the constitution: the two persons may occupy one degree among the different degrees of balance proper to the human species, or neighbouring degrees with no intermediate degree between them. Each class of generated things—mineral, vegetable, animal and human—has its distinctive constitution; each species within a class, each subgroup, and each individual also has its proper constitution. If the constitution required for a species disappears, that kind of individual cannot persist. The species-wide temperament thus comprehends a range of variations in individual and subgroup temperaments, and similarity or adjacency within this range establishes the relevant affinity.\n\nThis affinity has special significance, says the commentator, for the relation of spiritual pupils to masters, for their capacity to benefit one another, and for the attraction of one to another. The connection is not commonly understood even experientially among guides. For human spirits become individually determined from spiritual ranks—the intellects and souls—and are differentiated in nobility according to the greater or lesser interposition of other ranks. Fewer and weaker intermediaries mean that the rulings of possibility are less numerous and more attenuated. More powerful or more numerous mediations mean stronger and more numerous limitations. After God's decree, the mixture's degree of equilibrium conditions the manner in which a spirit is determined and manifested in the embodied person.\n\nA temperament in which the opposed elemental tendencies are more completely harmonized approximates unity, and is therefore suited to receiving a nobler spirit. The closest approach to true equilibrium is described as the centre of the circle within which perfect souls are determined, a point at which the elemental tendencies are brought into complete balance. Al-Mahāʾimī marks this as differing from some philosophers' account of equilibrium. The spirit is received according to that degree of suitability, whether it derives, in the cosmology assumed here, from the intellects or from the higher souls. A temperament further removed from the centre corresponds to a lower degree of spiritual manifestation. [Continued p. 181.]",
