      "old_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The further the constitution is from genuine equilibrium, the lower the rank of the spirit it is apt to manifest, according to the gradations presupposed by this cosmology.\n\n**Qūnawī:** Know and understand what I have said about a shared temperament, and by understanding it ascend to knowledge of the affinity proper to spirits under the other aspect, the one analogous to the hidden and purely divine intrinsic affinity.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The second human affinity, the one corresponding to the affirmative affinity between human and Real, consists in sharing spiritual qualities, elevations of station, and degrees of realization. This too is related to temperament under the model just described, for a spirit connected with a higher source is more encompassing of the descriptions of necessity, while one bound to a lower determination bears more of the rulings of possibility. Where the two forms of affinity are joined, the individuals share in more complete humanity. Understand.\n\n**Qūnawī:** If you know this through witnessing or through a realized understanding, you will perceive that some spirits have their first station of determination at the Preserved Tablet, others in the spirituality of the Throne from the station of Isrāfīl, others at the Footstool from the station of Mīkāʾīl, and others at the Lote Tree from the station of Jibrīl; and thus in a descending order to the lowest heaven, associated with Ismāʿīl, chief of its angels—peace be upon them all. Then you will recognize that the principal condition of the different ranks of human spirits, after God's prior knowledge, providence, decree and will, is what has just been described concerning temperaments, their closeness to or distance from the point of genuine equilibrium. The divine providence and will are displayed through the sound formation of the bodily constitution, which is followed by the breathing of spirit and its becoming determined. Understand and remember.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The text connects the spiritual ranks with an ordered account of cosmic spiritual principles. The first station of some spirits is the Preserved Tablet, considered in the degree to which their determination becomes perfected through equilibrium. The commentator explains the Tablet as the universal soul, related in one respect to primordial nature and in another to the First Intellect. As an intelligible principle of the balance of constitution it is compared to the heart of the whole world. For that reason Qūnawī does not attach this first case to the spirit presiding over a particular sphere. [Continued p. 182.]",
      "new_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The further the constitution is from genuine equilibrium, the lower the rank of the spirit it is apt to manifest, according to the gradations presupposed by this cosmology.\n\n**Qūnawī:** Know and understand what I have said about a shared temperament, and by understanding it ascend to knowledge of the affinity proper to spirits under the other aspect, the one analogous to the hidden and purely divine intrinsic affinity.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The second human affinity, the one corresponding to the affirmative affinity between human and Real, consists in sharing spiritual qualities, elevations of station, and degrees of realization. This is so whether the original determination comes from the Tablet or from above it. Perfection through equilibrium, however, is not connected with what lies above the Tablet, because the Tablet is the Universal Soul, called the green emerald.       "old_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** Other spirits are associated with the spirituality of the Throne, including the orders of angels connected with the station of Isrāfīl; other ranks are related to the Lote Tree and Jibrīl, to the heaven of the fixed stars and Riḍwān, to Saturn and its spiritual orders, to Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and finally the Moon and the lowest heaven. The text records a traditional cosmological hierarchy in which angelic names are assigned to these spheres; the commentator refers the detailed designation of their orders to Ibn ʿArabī's *ʿUqlat al-mustawfiz*. This is an exposition of the hierarchical imagery of the text, not a demonstration of astronomy.\n\nThe principal condition of an individual's spiritual place within this hierarchy is, in the model set out, the degree of the embodied constitution's equilibrium, though the author also acknowledges other secondary conditions, including celestial cycles, places and parental circumstances. Hence Qūnawī's injunctions to **understand** and **remember**: knowing the ordered spiritual types should lead the reader back to affinity among persons, including their sharing in spiritual characteristics and stations.\n\n**Qūnawī (beginning of the next distinction):** Rank-based affinity, by contrast, is not of one kind only but has a number of aspects.       "new_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The determination of some spirits begins from the spirituality of the Throne—the Throne of the All-Merciful—and the spirituality of the angels called the *Wāhibāt*, arising from the station of Isrāfīl. Thereafter some arise from the spirituality of the Lote Tree of the Furthest Limit, the limit of the station of worshippers, below the Footstool in the sphere of the zodiac, and from the angels named in connection with Jibrīl's station. Some arise from the spirituality of the sphere of the fixed stars: the *Tāliyāt*, from the station of Riḍwān, keeper of the gardens. Some arise from the spirituality of Saturn: the *Nāziʿāt*, from the station of the angel al-Karīm. Some arise from the spirituality of Jupiter: the *Mulqiyāt*, from the station of the angel al-Muqarrab. Some arise from the spirituality of Mars: the *Fāriqāt*, from the station of al-Khāshiʿ. Some arise from the spirituality of the Sun: the *Ṣifāt*, from the station of al-Rafīʿ. Some arise from the spirituality of Venus: the *Fāniyāt*, from the station of al-Ḥamd. Some arise from the spirituality of Mercury: the *Nāshiṭāt*, from the station of the angel al-Rūḥ. Some arise from the spirituality of the Moon: the spiritual angels, from the station of Ismāʿīl—peace be upon him. The names of these angels were mentioned by the perfect and perfecting Shaykh Muḥyī al-Dīn Ibn ʿArabī—may God sanctify his spirit—in the treatise *ʿUqlat al-mustawfiz*. [Reading note: the unusual order-names are transliterated as printed in this edition; they have not been replaced by conjectured canonical forms.]\n\n**Qūnawī:** You will then recognize ...\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** That is, when you know what we have mentioned through witnessing or verified understanding, you recognize that the greatest condition of the differing nobility or baseness of human spirits is the proximity or distance of temperaments from the point of genuine equilibrium.       "source_printed_page": 182,
      "old_arabic_transcription": "ومبدأ تعين بعضها روحانية العرش ، أي عرش الرحمن وروحانية الملائكة الواهبات ، وهي حاصلة من مقام إسرافيل عليه السلام ، وبعدها من روحانية سدرة المنتهى ، منتهى مقام العابدين تحت الكرسي في فلك البروج ، وهي الملائكة المسماة من مقام جبرائيل عليه السلام ، وبعضها من روحانية فلك الثوابت ، وهي التاليات من مقام رضوان خازن الجنان عليه السلام ، وبعضها من روحانية فلك زحل ، وهي النازعات من مقام الملك الكريم ، وبعضها من روحانية فلك المشتري ، \nوهي الملقيات من مقام الملك المقرب ، وبعضها من روحانية فلك المريخ ، وهي الفارقات من مقام الخاشع ، وبعضها من روحانية فلك الشمس ، وهي الصفات من مقام الرفيع ، وبعضها من روحانية فلك الزهرة ، وهي الفانيات من مقام الحمد ، وبعضها من روحانية عطارد ، وهي الناشطات من مقام فلك الروح ، وبعضها من روحانية فلك القمر ، وهي ملائكة الروحانية من مقام إسماعيل عليه السلام ، وأسامي هذه الملائكة ذكرها الشيخ الكامل المكمل محيي الدين بن العربي - قدس اللّه روحه - في رسالة  “ عقلة المستوفز \" 1 \" . \n\nقال المصنف رضي اللّه عنه : [ فتعرف حالة إذ ] أي : حالة إذ يعرف ما ذكرنا عن شهود ، أو فهم محقق إن الشرط الأكبر قيد به ؛ لأن لهذا التفاوت شرطا آخر من الأدوار الفلكية ، وخواص الأمكنة أحوال الأبوين لتفاوت أرواح الناس في الشرف والخسة ، هو قرب الأمزجة من نقطة الاعتدال الحقيقي وبعدها عنها ، \nلكن ذلك بعد سابق علم اللّه المسمى بالعناية والقضاء والمشيئة ، جعله بعدها ؛ لأنه أثر المزاج الذي هو أثر العناية التي هي المشيئة ؛ لأن أثرها يختص بحسب التسوية الربانية المسماة الاعتدال ، ربانية لحصولها من الرتبة الإلهية ، يليها نفخ الروح الذي هو تعين الروح لما فيه من الخروج من مقامه الغيبي إلى الظهور الذي هو التعين.\n \nفلذلك قال : [ فافهم ] ، وإنما قال : وتذكر لتعرف بذلك التناسب الذّاتي من الوجه الآخر ، وذلك باستجماع خواص تلك الملائكة ، وعينه . \n\nقال الشيخ رضي اللّه عنه : [ وأما المناسبة المرتبية ، فإنها ليست من وجه واحد ، بل من وجوه متعددة : أحدها من جهة معدنها الأصلية التي هي مبدأ تعينات الأرواح المشار إليها آنفا ،",
      "new_arabic": "ومبدأ تعين بعضها روحانية العرش ، أي عرش الرحمن وروحانية الملائكة الواهبات ، وهي حاصلة من مقام إسرافيل عليه السلام ، وبعدها من روحانية سدرة المنتهى ، منتهى مقام العابدين تحت الكرسي في فلك البروج ، وهي الملائكة المسماة من مقام جبرائيل عليه السلام ، وبعضها من روحانية فلك الثوابت ، وهي التاليات من مقام رضوان خازن الجنان عليه السلام ، وبعضها من روحانية فلك زحل ، وهي النازعات من مقام الملك الكريم ، وبعضها من روحانية فلك المشتري ، \nوهي الملقيات من مقام الملك المقرب ، وبعضها من روحانية فلك المريخ ، وهي الفارقات من مقام الخاشع ، وبعضها من روحانية فلك الشمس ، وهي الصفات من مقام الرفيع ، وبعضها من روحانية فلك الزهرة ، وهي الفانيات من مقام الحمد ، وبعضها من روحانية عطارد ، وهي الناشطات من مقام الملك الروح ، وبعضها من روحانية فلك القمر ، وهي ملائكة الروحانية من مقام إسماعيل عليه السلام ، وأسامي هذه الملائكة ذكرها الشيخ الكامل المكمل محيي الدين بن العربي - قدس اللّه روحه - في رسالة  “ عقلة المستوفز \" 1 \" . \n\nقال المصنف رضي اللّه عنه : [ فتعرف حالة إذ ] أي : حالة إذ يعرف ما ذكرنا عن شهود ، أو فهم محقق إن الشرط الأكبر قيد به ؛ لأن لهذا التفاوت شرطا آخر من الأدوار الفلكية ، وخواص الأمكنة أحوال الأبوين لتفاوت أرواح الناس في الشرف والخسة ، هو قرب الأمزجة من نقطة الاعتدال الحقيقي وبعدها عنها ، \nلكن ذلك بعد سابق علم اللّه المسمى بالعناية والقضاء والمشيئة ، جعله بعدها ؛ لأنه أثر المزاج الذي هو أثر العناية التي هي المشيئة ؛ لأن أثرها يختص بحسب التسوية الربانية المسماة الاعتدال ، ربانية لحصولها من الرتبة الإلهية ، يليها نفخ الروح الذي هو تعين الروح لما فيه من الخروج من مقامه الغيبي إلى الظهور الذي هو التعين.\n \nفلذلك قال : [ فافهم ] ، وإنما قال : وتذكر لتعرف بذلك التناسب الذّاتي من الوجه الآخر ، وذلك باستجماع خواص تلك الملائكة ، وعينه . \n\nقال الشيخ رضي اللّه عنه : [ وأما المناسبة المرتبية ، فإنها ليست من وجه واحد ، بل من وجوه متعددة : أحدها من جهة معدنها الأصلية التي هي مبدأ تعينات الأرواح المشار إليها آنفا ،",
      "arabic_correction_evidence": "2008 scan printed p182, PDF index180; scan_p182.png. The image reads من مقام الملك الروح, not the digital فلك الروح."
    },
    {
      "page": 183,
      "entry_id": "MSH-P183",
      "old_english": "**Qūnawī (continuing):** ...the original sources from which spirits are determined. The source of the highest of them, that is, the spirits of the perfected, is the Mother of the Book (*umm al-kitāb*). The first determination of certain others, in knowledge and in an existence comprehended under unity, is the reality of the Supreme Pen, called the First Intellect and Universal Spirit. Some are determined from the Preserved Tablet, others from the spirituality of the Throne associated with Isrāfīl, some from the spirituality of the Footstool associated with Mīkāʾīl, and others from the rank of Jibrīl at the Lote Tree. This ordering continues down through the types of these spiritual principles to the lowest heaven, whose spiritual chief Ismāʿīl corresponds to what the Peripatetic philosophers call the Active Intellect.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** In treating rank-based affinities, Qūnawī chooses three of their many possible aspects: the source from which the ranks begin, their mode or locus of appearance, and the intermediate stage connecting those beginnings with their manifestations. The first aspect therefore concerns the original *mines* or sources of spirits, not their subsequent perfection. He had previously distinguished the beginning of a spirit's determination from the station at which it becomes complete.\n\nThe perfected human spirits—those of prophets, poles and solitary realized individuals—begin from the Mother of the Book, explained here as divine knowledge in its comprehensive rather than differentiated consideration. It is the origin of origins in relation to the intellect and soul, themselves called divine books in the language of this cosmology. The *book* can also signify the great cosmos, whose intelligible principle is knowledge. The beings determined through the Supreme Pen or First Intellect receive a more unfolded mode of determination, one actually distinguished from what is below it while still united by comparison with subordinate ranks. The Pen is so called because of the image of writing and inscription; it is Intellect as comprehending things intelligibly and Universal Spirit as a principle to which lesser spiritual determinations are related.\n\nOther spirits belong to the Tablet, to the Throne and its spiritual orders, to the Footstool, to the Lote Tree, and to further angelic and celestial ranks. Qūnawī's invocation of the Active Intellect at the lowest heaven is intended to bring the hierarchical account into comparison with the philosophers. Al-Mahāʾimī disputes the view that the Active Intellect's action is simply confined to the elemental world. The references to the Peripatetics here belong to a medieval reconstruction of philosophical lineage and cosmology, not to an independently established history of Aristotle and Plato. [Continued p. 184.]",
      "new_english": "**Qūnawī (continuing):** ...the original sources from which spirits are determined. The source of the highest of them, that is, the spirits of the perfected, is the Mother of the Book (*umm al-kitāb*). The first determination of certain others, in knowledge and in an existence comprehended under unity, is the reality of the Supreme Pen, called the First Intellect and Universal Spirit. Some are determined from the Preserved Tablet, others from the spirituality of the Throne associated with Isrāfīl, some from the spirituality of the Footstool associated with Mīkāʾīl, and others from the rank of Jibrīl at the Lote Tree. This ordering continues down through the types of these spiritual principles to the lowest heaven, whose spiritual chief Ismāʿīl corresponds to what the Peripatetic philosophers call the Active Intellect.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Know that from the many aspects he selected three: that through which the beginning occurs, that toward which the end is directed, and that on which the middle depends. The first concerns their original sources, meaning the principles of their original determination without considering their perfection. It was indicated above that the principles of determination in respect of origin are the very principles in respect of perfection.\n\nHe then explains that the source of the determination of the highest spirits—the spirits of the perfected, among prophets, poles and solitary individuals—is the Mother of the Book, namely comprehensive divine knowledge. It is so called because it is the origin of origins for intellects and soul, which are divine books: the “book” here means the great cosmos, and knowledge is its origin. The determination of some begins in a differentiated manner under one aspect of their existence, while being comprehensive under another. This unity is relative to what lies beneath it. Existence here is actual, unlike at the first rank. Its source is the reality of the Supreme Pen itself, without the Preserved Tablet's relation to it. It is called Pen because through it the cosmos is recorded and inscribed; Intellect because it first understands the whole, being first in rank among creatures; Spirit because through it the cosmos is governed; and Universal because the universal spirits are its particulars. [Reading note: the print's explanation of the name “Pen” has the apparent error قلبًا, “heart,” in place of قلمًا.]\n\nSome spirits are of the Throne and of Isrāfīl, that is, from its soul and intellect together. The names are elucidated so that one does not imagine that these principles possess other things through which the stated affinity arises. He also indicates that these are the spiritual principles and their genera. At the end he calls [the principle of the lowest heaven] the Active Intellect to deny the claim that the Active Intellect is related only to the world of the elements.\n\nThe Peripatetics are a group of philosophers whose earliest members learned from Plato while on the road, according to what al-Sayyid al-Samarqandī mentions in his commentary on the *Ṣaḥāʾif*. [This is the commentator's historical claim.]\n\n**Qūnawī:** The other aspect concerns their imaginal manifestations, for spirits ... [continued on p. 184].",
      "reasons": [
        "Correct the reversal in the gloss: the print says the principles as origin are the same as those as perfection, whereas inherited English said the author had distinguished them.",
        "Restore omitted actual existence, the functions behind Pen/Intellect/Spirit/Universal, the specific account of Throne-related spirits and the closing Qūnawī lemma.",
        "Restore the commentator’s statement about the Peripatetics and Plato with its attribution to al-Samarqandī, replacing an added historical disclaimer that had displaced the source.",
        "Facsimile p183 checked; the printed apparent قلبًا error is noted explicitly and the overall interpretation follows the heading القلم."

    {
      "page": 184,
      "entry_id": "MSH-P184",
      "old_english": "**Qūnawī:** Another aspect of affinity is through the spirits' imaginal loci of manifestation. Spirits, despite their unequal ranks, are never without the loci through which they become determined and appear, according to all the realized knowers. The first rank in which human spirits appear, apart from the perfected, is the **absolute imaginal world** (*ʿālam al-mithāl al-muṭlaq*).\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This is the second aspect among the selected kinds of rank-based affinity. It concerns the starting-point of outward appearance, rather than the original spiritual source considered in itself. The absolute imaginal world is the realm in which spirits may appear through perceptible forms without gross bodies and without requiring the particular faculty of imagination lodged in an individual person's brain. Such forms make distinct appearances possible without reducing the spirit to elemental matter.\n\nThe commentator offers a philosophical argument: spirits, considered without any manifesting loci, are simple realities. If they were all of one specific kind without a way of acquiring determinate forms, their differences would not be enough to distinguish individuals as individuals. Merely appealing to different ranks would not fully resolve the problem, because a rank is a general condition rather than the particular determination of an individual. Individual characteristics do not become actual externally before manifestation. The imaginal loci provide the level at which distinct appearances become intelligible and visible. Apart from the perfected human spirits, which are treated as having a higher mode of determination, human spirits first acquire such manifestations in the absolute imaginal world. The commentator refers to Ibn ʿArabī's *ʿUqlat al-mustawfiz* for a corresponding cosmographical account.\n\n**Qūnawī:** Imaginal forms may take their originating material from the subtleties of the powers of this natural life and from its purified and refined substances clothed in the qualities of spirits. Yet their descriptions and states in Paradise are manifested according to their spiritualities and powers and according to the properties of their imaginal loci.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This indicates that the imaginal world both supplies and receives the loci through which the spirits of the people of Paradise appear. The natural human faculties involved are the animal powers, including outer and inner senses, and the vegetative faculties, as these are refined by righteous acts and noble character. The heart and the soul likewise contribute their refined subtleties, insofar as the heart is purified of domination by the commanding lower soul and the soul is refined in its traits. [Continued p. 185.]",
      "new_english": "**Qūnawī (continuing):** ...despite their unequal ranks, are never without the loci through which they become determined and appear, according to all the realized knowers. The first rank in which human spirits appear, apart from the perfected, is the **absolute imaginal world** (*ʿālam al-mithāl al-muṭlaq*).\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This is the second aspect among the selected kinds of rank-based affinity. It concerns the starting-point of outward appearance, rather than the original spiritual source considered in itself. The absolute imaginal world is the realm in which spirits may appear through perceptible forms without gross bodies and without requiring the particular faculty of imagination lodged in an individual person's brain. Such forms make distinct appearances possible without reducing the spirit to elemental matter.\n\nThe argument is that, without loci of manifestation, spirits could not be distinguished, because they are simple and one in species. Without such loci, their distinction would require a differentia added to the genus in which their specific unity is shared; what accounts for unity differs from what accounts for distinction. Differences of rank do not suffice, since they belong to general accidents. Nor do specific properties yield individual distinction. Particular accidents do not attach before manifestation. The first rank of manifestation of spirits other than those of the perfected is therefore the absolute imaginal world: before it they possess no determination of the kind reserved for the perfected, and appearance cannot precede determination. This world is in the sphere of the zodiac, according to what the verifying Shaykh Muḥyī al-Dīn Ibn ʿArabī—may God sanctify his mystery—mentions in his *ʿUqla*.\n\n**Qūnawī:** Imaginal forms may take their originating material from the subtleties of the powers of this natural life and from its purified and refined substances clothed in the qualities of spirits. Yet their descriptions and states in Paradise are manifested according to their spiritualities and powers and according to the properties of their imaginal loci.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This indicates that the imaginal world both supplies and receives the loci through which the spirits of the people of Paradise appear. The natural human faculties involved are the animal powers, including outer and inner senses, and the vegetative faculties, as these are refined by righteous acts and noble character. [Continued p. 185.]",
      "reasons": [

    {
      "page": 185,
      "entry_id": "MSH-P185",
      "old_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The heart and soul, once purified and made suitable, acquire qualities corresponding to spiritual forms. The forms found in Paradise are related to them; yet the specific qualities and changes of those forms in Paradise are not merely the direct persistence of earthly matter. They manifest according to the powers of the spirits and the properties of their imaginal bodies. Their capacity to change without the generation and corruption that characterize elemental bodies is adduced as evidence that the relevant level is the imaginal realm. In this way the imaginal world is both the place to which the outward forms of spirits are referred and the source from which they become manifest.\n\n**Qūnawī:** The dwellings of the people of Paradise are manifestations of the ranks of their spirits, both in respect of those spirits' standing before the Real and in respect of their first imaginal loci. The Prophet indicated this through subtle allusions, as when he is reported to have said to ʿAlī that his palace in Paradise would be opposite, or alongside, the Prophet's palace, and similarly concerning al-ʿAbbās. He also spoke of the people of faith as recognizing their dwellings in Paradise more readily than they recognize their homes in this world. This is a consequence of affinity.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The dwellings themselves therefore participate in the imaginal differentiation of the inhabitants: the purer or more attenuated the imaginal locus, the more appropriate its dwelling, without requiring the outward position of the dwelling to correspond identically to its occupant's spiritual station. The distinction matters in the report about ʿAlī's palace being opposite the Prophet's. The Prophet's spiritual rank exceeds that of even the highest saints. Mere physical or imaginal adjacency does not imply equality or near equality of spiritual station. The comparable statement about al-ʿAbbās makes this even clearer. Proximity in the configuration of a dwelling is one kind of relation, proximity in spiritual rank another. Qūnawī calls the reports subtle indications for precisely this reason.\n\n*Source-critical flag:* The online edition includes editorial footnotes saying the editor was unable to locate the particular palace reports about ʿAlī. They are transmitted here as **attributions in the medieval text**, not verified Prophetic sayings. The alternative wording about an adjacent palace should not be reproduced in a definitive edition as an established ḥadīth without an independent isnād search. [Discussion continues p. 186.]",
      "new_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** ...and the subtleties of its substances, namely the heart and soul, on condition that the heart is purified of the stain of the commanding soul and the soul is purified of its attributes and dispositions, so that these substances acquire the qualities of spirits and the paradisal forms accord with them. Yet those forms have states and qualities in Paradise that appear only according to their spiritualities and powers embodied in imaginal form, and according to the properties of their imaginal manifestations. The evidence is their transformation and alteration without generation and corruption. The qualities and states of those forms therefore belong to the imaginal world. Since this world is the return of the manifestations of spirits, it is also their beginning. He then returns to explaining affinity among people through this.\n\n**Qūnawī:** The dwellings of the people of Paradise manifest the ranks of their spirits, in respect of their standing before the Real and in respect of their first imaginal manifestations. The Prophet—God bless him and grant him peace—indicated this by subtle allusions, such as his saying, “ʿAlī, your palace in Paradise faces my palace”; in another narration, “is alongside my palace.” He said something similar concerning al-ʿAbbās. Concerning the generality of believers he said, “One of you knows the way to his dwelling in Paradise better than to his dwelling in this world.” This is nothing other than the ruling of affinity.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** He indicates that, just as the imaginal world is the return of the manifestations of the spirits of the people of Paradise in respect of the purity of their forms and states, it is also the return of their dwellings. This demonstrates still more clearly that it is the beginning of their manifestations. The dwellings of the people of Paradise are the ranks of their spirits appearing therein, in respect of their standing before the Real: their proximity or distance through affinity with Him. Their dwellings rise or descend accordingly, and according to their imaginal manifestations, which are the first manifestations. The dwelling accords with whether a person's imaginal form is purer or more turbid.\n\nHe adduces the Prophet's saying to ʿAlī, “Your palace in Paradise faces my palace.” For proximity of ʿAlī's spiritual standing to that of the Prophet is not possible: the lowest rank of the prophets is above the highest rank of the saints, and he is the most excellent of the prophets. Where, then, is his standing in relation to ʿAlī's? It must therefore be in respect of ... [continued on p. 186].\n\n**Editorial source note:** The modern editor says he could not locate either wording of the palace report to ʿAlī. The reports above are translated as attributions in the medieval text; this review has not independently verified their transmission.",
      "reasons": [

    {
      "page": 186,
      "entry_id": "MSH-P186",
      "old_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The report about faithful people finding their dwellings makes the distinction between spiritual rank and imaginal location clearer. He therefore returns to the general principle that all of these are rulings of appropriate relation or affinity.\n\n**Qūnawī:** As for the market of Paradise, in which beautiful human forms are offered and the inhabitants of Paradise may assume whichever of them they desire, it proceeds from a particular channel of the absolute imaginal world, the source and spring of manifestations. Through this channel help flows from the imaginal world to the loci through which the spirits of the people of Paradise appear.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This answers a possible objection. The original imaginal form was said to arise through the refined faculties and character acquired during earthly life, together with the spirit's powers and the properties of its first imaginal locus. Those characteristics would have been settled at the person's death and resurrection; how, then, can the person adopt new appearances at will in the market? And how can a common market have a meaning beyond the specific dwellings already corresponding to individuals' degrees?\n\nThe earlier account concerned **principal forms** and **principal dwellings**. The additional forms, spaces and appearances may proceed as secondary manifestations from particular channels of the inexhaustible absolute imaginal world. Its unrestricted totality is like a great sea, whereas the subsidiary channels provide individualized streams of manifestation. The distinctions of principal rank need not be mirrored by identical distinctions in every subsidiary dwelling. Similarly, the settled properties of the first form need not exhaust the additional qualities that may become manifest through secondary forms. The notion of a channel is introduced to explain continuing supplies of manifestation suitable to distinct subjects. [Continued p. 187.]",
      "new_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** ...the imaginal manifestations. That is why he counted this among the subtle allusions. The other narration, “alongside my palace,” confirms it: alignment applies more directly to outward form, so this too subtly points to imaginal manifestations. Moreover, even were ʿAlī's standing near that of the Prophet, how could something similar hold for al-ʿAbbās? Nearness in imaginal manifestations is quite possible despite distance in standing before God. This is an affinity in sensible things and does not require affinity in realities related to the Real to precisely the same extent.\n\nHe then anticipates the objection that this account succeeds only if spiritual affinity is considered in those dwellings. He answers with the report concerning the generality of believers, “One of you knows the way better ...,” then states his point explicitly: “This is nothing other than the ruling of affinity.”\n\n**Qūnawī:** As for the market of Paradise, comprising beautiful human forms which its inhabitants may choose to put on as they wish, it belongs to some of the streams of the absolute imaginal world, the source and spring of manifestations. It is a channel of the sustaining influx that reaches the manifestations of the spirits of the people of Paradise from the imaginal world.\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This answers an implicit question. The materials of the imaginal form are the subtleties of the powers of this natural constitution and its purified substances; its attributes, and likewise its states, appear according to its spiritualities, powers and the properties of its imaginal manifestations. But the materials of the forms in the market are not the subtleties of those natural powers, which are fixed and do not change after death and resurrection. Nor are they attributes appearing from their spiritualities as they stand—adding that there is no need of *al-takharruj* [an unclear term in the printed sentence]. Nor do they come from the properties of their imaginal manifestations, for those have already appeared in the first forms. What, then, are these forms? Likewise, their dwellings manifest the ranks of spirits according to their standing before the Real and their imaginal manifestations. What is this market, which is one of their dwellings? It does not accord with their differing standing before the Real, since all share access to it; nor with their imaginal manifestations, which would require distinctions in this dwelling's appearance.\n\nHe answers that the first account concerns original forms and original dwellings, constituted from the sea of the absolute imaginal world. These other forms and dwellings are secondary, arising from some of that world's streams. The absolute imaginal world is a vast sea, the source of many manifestations and forms. The distinctions required in the original dwellings need not be required in the secondary ones; and the properties of their manifestations that appeared in ... [continued on p. 187].",

    {
      "page": 187,
      "entry_id": "MSH-P187",
      "old_english": "**Al-Mahāʾimī (continuing):** The supply of manifestation must continually reach the inhabitants because existence is ever renewed: at every moment there is a new creation.       "page": 62,
      "entry_id": "MSH-050",
      "old_english": "... existence. For this reason the primordial rank is sought for the sake of the Essence. The kind of knowledge intended by the creation of the world in the reported saying “I was a hidden treasure and loved to be known” is obtained only through a locus such as this, for it includes every self-disclosure; no one fully knows what is absent from his own constitution. The loftiest of the determinations is the first determination, in which the Essence discloses Itself to Itself under the attribute of oneness (*wāḥida*), where manifestation and hiddenness are in equilibrium. Because this determination is receptive to both, it is a locus for *aḥadiyya* and *wāḥidiyya*: the two are related, and their relation is displayed through that intervening unity. [The report “hidden treasure” is cited as a received saying, not verified as a prophetic ḥadīth.]\n\nThere are two considerations of the Essence: first, the negation of multiplicity and relations, under which It is named *Aḥad*; second, the consideration of these [relations], under which It is named *Wāḥid*. The first self-disclosure encompasses essential and nominal perfection in comprehensive, undifferentiated fashion. Complete differentiation of particulars requires the distinctness of realities, for which there is no room in the first disclosure owing to the preponderance of unity. Essential perfection entails absolute self-sufficiency: the eternal comprehension of everything that is capable of differentiation to eternity in one all-inclusive witnessing, without dependence upon its differentiated unfolding.\n\nWhat is sought here, then, is the perfection of the Names, conditioned by the world in its differentiated aspect and by Adam as a comprehensive presence arising after that differentiation. The Essence demands this perfection insofar as It is qualified by Names and Attributes. Detailed differentiation is a further perfection that requires the realities to become distinguished and some rule of otherness to obtain—even if only as a relation. Neither is possible under *aḥadiyya* considered as such. Another determination is therefore required, in which divine, cosmic and human realities, and all that can be differentiated, become distinct: the **second determination and second self-disclosure**. Since it appears from the first determination in that determination's form, it comprises unity, multiplicity, an intermediary and a differentiating limit, just as the first includes unity and the two aspects *aḥadiyya* and *wāḥidiyya*. Its unity is called the outward face of existence, and its multiplicity the outward face of knowledge. Necessity accompanies the first, possibility the second. Manifest existence possesses true unity through the pervasion of *aḥadiyya* and relational plurality through the pervasion of *wāḥidiyya*; the outward face of knowledge has the reverse arrangement. Multiplicity in knowledge concerns the fixed entities of possibilities, while multiplicity of existence is the origin of the divine Names and Attributes. Existential unity encompasses primordial affairs; the unity of knowledge is the Presence of meanings and the sea of possibility. [This passage contains compressed antecedents and should be collated before its subdivisions are treated as a definitive taxonomy.]\n\nQūnawī's phrase “under the loftiest aspects of His primordial affairs and His highest determinations” thus indicates that no one can aspire to what lies beyond that rank. He will explicitly state this later in the text. Understand, and God is the Inspirer.",

      "page": 63,
      "entry_id": "MSH-051",
      "old_english": "**Qūnawī says:** “Thus He, exalted is He, is the very reality of their certain knowledge, its eye and its truth throughout the ranks of His essential knowledge, related first to Himself and then to His objects of knowledge, while they are effaced in Him as regards themselves, yet their ruling remains and His pervasion continues in all His existents and Presences.” **Al-Mahāʾimī explains:** Because the utmost reach of their aspirations is the noblest object of His knowledge, He is the reality of their knowledge of certainty. Because it is the highest object of His will, He is the reality of the eye of their certainty. When what they will coincides with what He wills through His Essence, He is the reality of the reality of their certainty.\n\nHere is the explanation. When their knowledge attains the noblest objects of eternal knowledge, they know the unity of all things in existence. They consequently know that their certain knowledge, considered in its existence, is the very true Existence. Yet at this rank their individual selves and their knowing still veil them. When knowledge becomes direct seeing, the veil of knowledge is lifted and they perceive that the eye of their certainty is true Existence itself. When direct seeing becomes realization through the Real and the spectator is effaced, they realize that He, **in respect of existence**, is the very reality of their certainty. **This is not said under the consideration of His unrestrictedness**: considered so, He is independent of the worlds and remains beyond the veil [of their knowledge]. Rather it is said under the distinct ranks of His essential knowledge, which, although essential, admits of ranks according as it relates first to the Essence and then to objects known.\n\nThis knowledge, relating to the Essence without the veil of the spectator's knowledge or individual self, is the reality of certainty attained by the elect. They attain it through self-effacement in Him, **not** by becoming nonexistent as spirit, soul or body, but by ceasing to apprehend these things under their own aspect. They apprehend them instead as shadows of the Real and lights manifest through His light. Hence their *rulings* remain even while their independent existence is effaced from awareness. Since these rulings remain, they continue to be knowers who have realized the reality of certainty. He is likewise the reality of their certainty insofar as He pervades all His existents and Presences, among which the reality of their certainty is included, as it belongs to the domain of knowledge.\n\nKnow that this pervasion (*sarāyān*) is **not** the pervasion of indwelling (*ḥulūl*). Indwelling would be like that of an accident in a substance; but God is no accident of anything, since accidents exist through Him—how could He be one of them? Nor is it like a form's inherence in matter: He is the form of nothing, for forms exist through Him and matter through their forms—how could He be identical with either? Nor is it an occupant's presence in a place, from which He is transcendent, since He encompasses the whole: how could a place encompass Him? Rather His pervasion is like the passage of sunlight through glass, without anything moving ...",

      "old_english": "... from the sun to the glass, as might be imagined. Rather the effect arises through the glass facing the sun: the light takes on the apparent colour of the glass, although sunlight itself has no colour. By the pervasion of the Presences he means manifestation at the first determination and in the subsequent ranks of eternal relations.\n\nThe learned Ṣadr al-Dīn says in the *Epistle on Unity*: “Then it”—that is, the unrestricted Identity—“required manifestation from the limit of the unseen to the limit of witnessing, and the realization of those attributes and determinations as distinguishable in the entities in actuality; it knows them distinctly and brought about the world of spirits, namely intellects and souls. The manifestation of existence there is more complete than in the world of meanings; then came the imaginal world and the world of bodies. In this world the manifestation of existence was completed, for the self-disclosure of existence attained completeness with the bringing into being of the first body which delimits the directions, the Throne, the station of establishment in divine discourse.”\n\n**Objection:** To say that [the absolute Identity] requires manifestation and that possibility exists as something able to receive its effect is impossible. If possibility is actual, it is either in existence, and hence necessary, or in a quiddity, which is nonexistent, known or unknown, even impossible; there is no third alternative. **Reply:** Its object and correlate should be considered with precision [the recorded «اليقين» is uncertain]. We deny that quiddities are unable to receive existence. If they are conjoined with existence, they necessarily become existent, and such conjunction is indeed possible. There are determinations whose natural subject is extramental existence, others whose natural subject is intelligible existence, and still others whose natural subject is unrestricted existence, as in the fixed entities. Nevertheless, these are not existent by an existence which is their own essence or an intrinsic constituent of them. If they were, the distinction between quiddity as such and knowledge or nonknowledge of it would be overturned. Whenever a quiddity becomes existent by conjunction with existence, its being-existent depends on its conjunction with existence, which is other than the quiddity.\n\nOne must not argue: if existence is necessary, everything that exists must be necessary. We reject the inference: existence is necessary precisely because it is actual through itself, unlike that which exists derivatively (*bi-l-ʿaraḍ*). The latter's being-existent is a conceptual attribution; for this reason negative attributes and privative accidents may also be predicated of it. Whoever regards ...",
      "new_english": "... from the sun to the glass, as might be imagined. Rather the effect arises through the glass facing the sun: the light takes on the apparent colour of the glass, although sunlight itself has no colour. By the pervasion of the Presences he means manifestation at the first determination and in the subsequent ranks of eternal relations.\n\nThe learned Ṣadr al-Dīn says in the *Epistle on Unity*: “Then it”—that is, the unrestricted Identity—“required manifestation from the limit of the unseen to the limit of witnessing, and the realization of those attributes and determinations as distinguishable in the entities in actuality; it knows them distinctly and brought about the world of spirits, namely intellects and souls. The manifestation of existence there is more complete than in the world of meanings; then came the imaginal world and the world of bodies. In this world the manifestation of existence was completed, for the self-disclosure of existence attained completeness with the bringing into being of the first body which delimits the directions, the Throne, the station of establishment in divine discourse.”\n\n**Objection:** To say that [the absolute Identity] requires manifestation and that possibility exists as something able to receive its effect is impossible. If possibility is actual, it is either in existence, and hence necessary, or in a quiddity, which is nonexistent, known or unknown, even impossible; there is no third alternative. **Reply:** Rather, its subject and correlate is “certainty” [اليقين, as printed; the reading and intended sense are uncertain]. We deny that quiddities are unable to receive existence. If they are conjoined with existence, they necessarily become existent, and such conjunction is indeed actual. There are determinations whose natural subject is extramental existence, others whose natural subject is intelligible existence, and still others whose natural subject is unrestricted existence, as in the fixed entities. Nevertheless, these are not existent by an existence which is their own essence or an intrinsic constituent of them. The following printed wording is unstable: “Otherwise it would follow from quiddity as such being neither unknown nor known; for the existent does not become caused and unknown.” [No independent witness has resolved this sentence.] Whenever a quiddity becomes existent by conjunction with existence, its being-existent depends on its conjunction with existence, which is other than the quiddity.\n\nOne must not argue: if existence is necessary, everything that exists must be necessary. We reject the inference: existence is necessary precisely because it is actual through itself, unlike that which exists derivatively (*bi-l-ʿaraḍ*). The latter's being-existent is a conceptual attribution; for this reason negative attributes and privative accidents may also be predicated of it. Whoever regards ...",

      "page": 66,
      "entry_id": "MSH-054",
      "old_english": "... nor the restrictions that naturally accompany it an obstacle to the remaining kinds of apprehension, most of which are attained through acquisition and free choice. Acquisition cannot take place without sensory apprehension. How, then, could sense perception in itself bar the other modes? It obstructs them only insofar as it draws the novice towards sensible things considered as ends in themselves; during the first stages effacement is necessary. **At the stage of abiding (*baqāʾ*), however, sense perception is no obstacle.**\n\nOne should not object: if these modes of apprehension are perfections, death would diminish them, whereas what is sought by the Necessary Essence is the manifestation of perfections and removal of defects; why, then, do perfected people die? We reply that death completes their perfection, for perfected souls remain capable after death of everything they were capable of before, including sensory apprehension. Establishing this fully would require more explanation than this brief work can contain. This concludes the substance of the learned author's discussion.\n\n**Qūnawī says:** “May God bless the one who has realized Him from the aspect of the most perfect witnessing and the most complete, noblest and most comprehensive knowledge, while constantly present with Him in all his stations, states, ranks and modes of being.”\n\nSince, under the divine customary ordering, the agent's efficacy upon a recipient requires a proportion or affinity between them, and the utterly transcendent Real cannot be directly proportioned to creation in its radical dependence, a mediator possessing both disengagement and connection is needed: he receives overflowing grace through the former aspect and conveys it through the latter. According to the realized masters, our Prophet most perfectly combines both. Qūnawī therefore seeks blessing through the most complete means, the invocation of blessings (*ṣalāt*), which is a relation joining the invoker and the one invoked. From God it is mercy, generosity and forgiveness; from creatures it is prayer and humble submission. The related roots ‘connection’, ‘bond’, ‘joining’, ‘warmth’ and ‘strength’ evoke the common idea of coming together and drawing near. The goal is that the Real appoint the Prophet as vicegerent so that he becomes one who follows the Real in manifesting His form, and that he be connected with the essential and nominal self-disclosures particular to divine election. Human reality is thereby linked to the five Presences from which it arises. The first is the Presence of his reality, corresponding to his fixed entity in divine knowledge. The second is his spirit—that is, the Breath of the All-Merciful determined through that fixed entity so as to give it relief from the constriction of its nonexistence. The third is his bodily form and individual person.",

      "old_english": "... his state: this is the eye of certainty. Qūnawī next explains that he is realized through the most complete knowledge, because he has access to eternal knowledge. It is called the noblest because nobility here consists in the absence or reduction of intermediaries; this indicates that no mediator stands between the Prophet's knowledge and eternal knowledge. It is called the most comprehensive because it encompasses limitless objects of knowledge. It is not called the most perfect because, considered as knowledge, it is one reality among divine realities, unlike his witnessing, which is comprehensive in all of its realities. Witnessing is not called the noblest because it embraces what is mediated and what is unmediated. This witnessing and knowledge belong to him without temporal interruption through his constant presence with his Lord; visions and self-disclosures follow continuously without a gap in which he becomes wholly occupied with another. The ‘stations’ are the five divine Presences; ‘states’ are the alterations of self-disclosure; ‘ranks’ are their order according to degrees of elevation and the sequence of mediations under the divine customary order; and ‘modes of being’ are renewed self-disclosures in all these at successive instants. True praise belongs to the One who raised him above them, with reference to his higher reality. Each divine name has a form in knowledge called a quiddity or fixed entity, and a form outside the mind called a locus of manifestation. The names are the lords of those loci. **The Muhammadan Reality** is the form of the Essence together with all the names; it is the image of the all-comprehensive name from which the overflow reaches all other names. This reality governs the intelligible form by means of the Lord who manifests in it, the Lord of lords, and thus has unrestricted lordship [by derivation and vicegerency].       "page": 70,
      "entry_id": "MSH-058",
      "old_english": "The community to whom he—peace be upon him—was sent consists, insofar as they answer him, of the community of response and acceptance of the summons, though the summons was originally universal. It is the former community that is intended, since the latter, as such, contains no elect. These are those whose souls have been purified of vices and whose hearts of their turbidity; God has purified them of [preoccupation with] their own existence and endowed them with [awareness of] His existence and attributes. He then mentions what follows from such purity: receiving the most complete inheritance, indicated by the Prophet's saying: “The learned are heirs of the prophets. The prophets leave neither dinar nor dirham; they bequeath only knowledge, and whoever takes it has taken an abundant portion.”\n\nBy saying “an abundant portion” he indicates that this is not merely a matter of the sciences of formal study; such study, by itself, does not yield the fullness of certain realization. Rather, it is knowledge bestowed directly from God (*ʿilm ladunnī*), obtained through the light of unveiling when the breast opens to knowledge of certainty, the eye of certainty, and the reality of certainty. This is why he says “embracing his sciences”: the real, universal sciences that entail their principles. States and stations are divine self-disclosures: insofar as they change and do not remain fixed they are states, and when they become firmly established they are stations. There is considerable disagreement here, which is not the place to pursue.\n\nHe [Qūnawī] said, may God be pleased with him: “[Together with their actual realization of the results of their distinctive shares, which distinguish them from those [shares] distinguished by the properties of intermediaries, the fruits of following, and the effects of connections.]”\n\nThat is, they inherit his fullest inheritance while realizing the consequences of their particular shares. A “result” is what arises from another thing as its offspring; specialists in rational inquiry reserve the term for what follows intrinsically from a proof. Here it means the knowledges, states, and stations consequent upon their distinctive shares. The plural *ḥuẓūẓ* means allotted portions, and here a disclosure particular to each according to his particular receptivity. “Particular” is what is found in one and not in others. If this exclusion extends to all others, the particularity is absolute, and the effusion is a disclosure whose genus, species, or attribute may otherwise be found elsewhere [the syntax of this clause is uncertain]. The restriction is needed because disclosures never recur numerically as the same individual disclosure, as the base text says. He distinguishes the particular shares from those set apart by the qualities of intermediaries. An intermediary conveys an agent's effect to a receptive patient; its own characteristics colour the effect, giving it properties it would not otherwise have. Such intermediary-specific shares are found in the recipient only through that intermediary. Likewise, they are distinguished from the shares—[sentence continues on p. 71].",
      "new_english": "The community to whom he—peace be upon him—was sent consists, insofar as they answer him, of the community of response and acceptance of the summons, though the summons was originally universal. It is the former community that is intended, since the latter, as such, contains no elect. These are those whose souls have been purified of vices and whose hearts of their turbidity; God has purified them of their own existence [and attributes] through His existence and attributes. [The printed phrase وأوصى فهم is corrupt; “and attributes” is a contextual conjecture, not an independently attested reading.] He then mentions what follows from such purity: receiving the most complete inheritance, indicated by the Prophet's saying: “The learned are heirs of the prophets. The prophets leave neither dinar nor dirham; they bequeath only knowledge, and whoever takes it has taken an abundant portion.”\n\nBy saying “an abundant portion” he indicates that this is not knowledge acquired by formal study, since the abundant portion and the coolness of certainty are not obtained through it. Rather, it is knowledge bestowed directly from God (*ʿilm ladunnī*), obtained through the light of unveiling when the breast opens to knowledge of certainty, the eye of certainty, and the reality of certainty. This is why he says “embracing his sciences”: the real, universal sciences that entail their principles. States and stations are divine self-disclosures: insofar as they change and do not remain fixed they are states, and when they become firmly established they are stations. There is considerable disagreement here, which is not the place to pursue.\n\nHe [Qūnawī] said, may God be pleased with him: “[Together with their actual realization of the results of their distinctive shares, which distinguish them from those [shares] distinguished by the properties of intermediaries, the fruits of following, and the effects of connections.]”\n\nThat is, they inherit his fullest inheritance while realizing the consequences of their particular shares. A “result” is what arises from another thing as its offspring; specialists in rational inquiry reserve the term for what follows intrinsically from a proof. Here it means the knowledges, states, and stations consequent upon their distinctive shares. The plural *ḥuẓūẓ* means allotted portions, and here a disclosure particular to each according to his particular receptivity. “Particular” is what is found in one and not in others. If this exclusion extends to all others, the particularity is absolute, and the effusion is a disclosure whose genus, species, or attribute may otherwise be found elsewhere [the syntax of this clause is uncertain]. The restriction is needed because disclosures never recur numerically as the same individual disclosure, as the base text says. He distinguishes the particular shares from those set apart by the qualities of intermediaries. An intermediary conveys an agent's effect to a receptive patient; its own characteristics colour the effect, giving it properties it would not otherwise have. Such intermediary-specific shares are found in the recipient only through that intermediary. Likewise, they are distinguished from the shares—[sentence continues on p. 71].",

      "page": 73,
      "entry_id": "MSH-061",
      "old_english": "“—and restriction. There is no doubt that conceiving any determination requires that non-determination precede it. Thus all that we have enumerated is incompatible with absoluteness.” [End of Qūnawī’s sentence begun p. 72.]\n\nLexically, *al-Ḥaqq* means the established or real. Unrestricted existence is called thus because it is established through itself, while everything else is established through it. Existence is established from every aspect, whereas what is other than it is not established in virtue of its own essence but only through another. To prohibit predication of it insofar as it possesses intrinsic absoluteness, even though it is the subject of all predications, is to say that the latter apply by reason of its many and different determinations and other aspects; the relevant consideration is determination rather than absoluteness. The qualifier “intrinsic” distinguishes this from the freedom of the first determination from the [differentiated] names: insofar as it is the first determination, it admits predications of unity, determination, knowledge of the essence, and necessity of existence.\n\nAn objection: “You have judged of it that no judgement can be made about it—is that not a contradiction? And you judge that it is unrestricted and describe it as absolute.”\n\nWe reply: what is intended is that this determined reality, considered before its determination, cannot then be subjected to that judgement. When it becomes determined and knowledge is related to it, one judges that it was not subject to judgement at that prior consideration, nor restricted or qualified. More fundamentally, the prohibition of judgement means that it cannot be bound by the judgement: the assertion and its opposite stand on an equal footing relative to it. A judgement is the relating of one thing to another. Definition by attributes is a descriptive (*rasmī*) definition, through which the Real may now be known, whereas a true essential definition is impossible in His case forever, beginninglessly and endlessly. “Attribute” here includes both affirmative and negative predicates; this kind of definition is impossible in the intrinsic respect because it is itself a form of judgement. Likewise, the assignment of a relation is precluded because a relation is a kind of identifying attribute. Unity here is not opposed to multiplicity but calls attention to negating the multiplicity wrongly imagined in Him. It cannot be attributed in that intrinsic respect because it is relational. The necessity of existence means that existence is from His essence—or identical with it—but assigning even this as a predicate invokes a relation based upon unity. “Principiality” means being the source of things: a relation based upon necessary existence. The requiring of existentiation is His manifestation of things in the mode of choice; the issuing forth of an effect is a wider expression, since it could also apply in a necessitarian mode. Both are relations consequent upon principiality.\n\nHe then mentions the one matter whose exclusion entails the exclusion of all the others: no relation of His knowledge to Himself or to another may be predicated insofar as He is considered absolutely unrestricted; the other descriptions depend on this relation. This emphatically does **not** mean that ignorance came first—God is infinitely exalted above that—but only that knowledge cannot be considered *together with this consideration of absoluteness*, just as these other matters cannot be taken together with it, despite being eternally necessary to the Real under their appropriate considerations. He then explains the whole by what explains their primary basis—[continued p. 74].",
      "new_english": "“—and restriction. There is no doubt that conceiving any determination requires that non-determination precede it. Thus all that we have enumerated is incompatible with absoluteness.” [End of Qūnawī’s sentence begun p. 72.]\n\nLexically, *al-Ḥaqq* means the established or real. Unrestricted existence is called thus because it is established through itself, while everything else is established through it. Existence is established from every aspect, whereas what is other than it is not established in virtue of its own essence but only through another. To prohibit predication of it insofar as it possesses intrinsic absoluteness, even though it is the subject of all predications, is to say that the latter apply by reason of its many and different determinations and other aspects; “consideration is given to determination in absoluteness,” as the print reads. [The context appears to require a negation, but no independent witness has been collated.] The qualifier “intrinsic” distinguishes this from the freedom of the first determination from the [differentiated] names: insofar as it is the first determination, it admits predications of unity, determination, knowledge of the essence, and necessity of existence.\n\nAn objection: “You have judged of it that no judgement can be made about it—is that not a contradiction? And you judge that it is unrestricted and describe it as absolute.”\n\nWe reply: what is intended is that this determined reality, considered before its determination, cannot then be subjected to that judgement. When it becomes determined and knowledge is related to it, one judges that it was not subject to judgement at that prior consideration, nor restricted or qualified. More fundamentally, the prohibition of judgement means that it cannot be bound by the judgement: the assertion and its opposite stand on an equal footing relative to it. A judgement is the relating of one thing to another. Definition by attributes is a descriptive (*rasmī*) definition, through which the Real may now be known, whereas a true essential definition is impossible in His case forever, beginninglessly and endlessly. “Attribute” here includes both affirmative and negative predicates; this kind of definition is impossible in the intrinsic respect because it is itself a form of judgement. Likewise, the assignment of a relation is precluded because a relation is a kind of identifying attribute. Unity here is not opposed to multiplicity but calls attention to negating the multiplicity wrongly imagined in Him. It cannot be attributed in that intrinsic respect because it is relational. The necessity of existence means that existence is from His essence—indeed, is His very essence—but assigning even this as a predicate invokes a relation based upon unity. “Principiality” means being the source of things: a relation based upon necessary existence. The requiring of existentiation is His manifestation of things in the mode of choice; the issuing forth of an effect is a wider expression, since it could also apply in a necessitarian mode. Both are relations consequent upon principiality.\n\nHe then mentions the one matter whose exclusion entails the exclusion of all the others: no relation of His knowledge to Himself or to another may be predicated insofar as He is considered absolutely unrestricted; the other descriptions depend on this relation. This emphatically does **not** mean that ignorance came first—God is infinitely exalted above that—but only that knowledge cannot be considered *together with this consideration of absoluteness*, just as these other matters cannot be taken together with it, despite being eternally necessary to the Real under their appropriate considerations. He then explains the whole by what explains their primary basis—[continued p. 74].",
      "reasons": [

        "Render بل عين ذاته as an intensifying correction, indeed His very essence, not an alternative or identical with it.",

    {
      "page": 74,
      "entry_id": "MSH-062",
      "old_english": "—and of its consequences: each description entails specification and restriction. For what is not specified, how could a determinate judgement be asserted, a determinate attribute assigned, or a determinate relation added? He next gives the reason for considering absoluteness: the conception of any determination necessarily presupposes non-determination. Judgements, descriptive definitions, and attributed relations therefore conflict with the absoluteness conceived prior to determination. Every determination is a restriction that comes after [its basis in the order of consideration], and what precedes all determinations is nothing other than non-determination. Understand.\n\nHe [Qūnawī] said, may God be pleased with him: “[Rather, to conceive the Real's absoluteness it must be conceived as a negative attribute, not as an absoluteness whose opposite is restriction. It is freedom from the familiar unity and multiplicity, and from confinement to either absoluteness or restriction, or their combination, or transcendence of them all. Thus all these may properly be asserted of Him while He transcends them all. Ascribing each of these or its contrary to Him, or negating it of Him, stands equally: neither side has priority over the other.]” The ordinary absoluteness opposed to restriction is itself one of the qualified judgements dependent upon determination.\n\nThus, he says, to conceive this absoluteness one must conceive it negatively: that He is not bound by anything, not that He possesses the ordinary absoluteness opposed to restriction. The term is used because He is free from the commonly known unity and multiplicity. From the standpoint of absoluteness He is not restricted by either; it is His degrees and determinations that are so qualified. Likewise He is free from confinement to absoluteness and determination, though these pertain in their different respects to His degrees and determinations. Nor is He confined to their conjunction—unity, multiplicity, absoluteness and restriction—even though all are present relative to those degrees. Hence ascribing any of these to Him, or ascribing other predicates—transcendence and likeness, unseen and witnessed—or denying them, are equally possible without one pole prevailing. Were one pole to prevail in this unrestricted regard, He would become conditioned by it, and a subordinate pole would not stand on the same footing. Priority among predicates obtains only according to ranks dependent upon determinations; these have no force where intrinsic absoluteness is the consideration. Understand: this is a place where the feet easily slip.",

      "page": 76,
      "entry_id": "MSH-064",
      "old_english": "He [Qūnawī] said: “[The unity of the Real becomes intelligible].” This unity is an essential relation considered as the negation of multiplicity from Him intrinsically; it cannot be considered in the unqualified Essence, which holds good with [descriptions of] unity and multiplicity. The same applies to His necessity of existence: this is a relation, the Essence of existence requiring [existence], considered with a distinction only in thought, as mentioned before. It is not considered in unrestricted absoluteness, which also encompasses the possible things. The same applies to His principiality, since that is a relation between Him and what He brings forth and cannot be considered in unrestricted absoluteness, which encompasses what is brought forth. These relations appear under the first determination. Before knowledge [in the order of apprehension] none can be understood: if He did not know His essence, how would its unity be judged? Without knowledge of unity, how would necessity be judged, given the impossibility of multiple necessary beings? Without knowledge of necessity, how would principiality toward multiplicity be known? And without knowledge of necessity, how could He be known as both the origin and the end of events? More specifically, conceiving each of these depends upon the intrinsic knowledge-relation, insofar as His knowledge of Himself within Himself adds nothing to His essence; through it He knows His unity. Without this, unity from every aspect would not be intelligible, since otherwise Essence and attribute would constitute a multiplicity. Similarly, the necessity of existence depends—[continued p. 77].",
      "new_english": "He [Qūnawī] said: “[The unity of the Real becomes intelligible].” This unity is an essential relation considered as the negation of multiplicity from Him intrinsically; it can [not] be considered in the unqualified Essence, which holds good with [descriptions of] unity and multiplicity. The same applies to His necessity of existence: this is a relation, the Essence of existence requiring [existence], considered with a distinction only in thought, as mentioned before. It is [not] considered in unrestricted absoluteness, which also encompasses the possible things. The same applies to His principiality, since that is a relation between Him and what He brings forth and cannot be considered in unrestricted absoluteness, which encompasses what is brought forth. These relations appear under the first determination. Before knowledge [in the order of apprehension] none can be understood: if He did not know His essence, how would its unity be judged? Without knowledge of unity, how would necessity be judged, given the impossibility of multiple necessary beings? Without knowledge of necessity, how would principiality toward multiplicity be known? And without knowledge of necessity, how could He be known as both the origin and the end of events? More specifically, conceiving each of these depends upon the intrinsic knowledge-relation, insofar as His knowledge of Himself within Himself adds nothing to His essence; through it He knows His unity. Without this, unity from every aspect would not be intelligible, since otherwise Essence and attribute would constitute a multiplicity. Similarly, the necessity of existence depends—[continued p. 77].\n\n**Reading note:** The first two negative statements above require contextual supplementation: the 2008 print reads والاعتبار لها, without an explicit negative. The third parallel statement explicitly reads ولا اعتبار لها. The bracketed negatives follow that parallel and the argument, not a separately collated witness.",
      "reasons": [
        "Expose the contextual negations silently supplied by the inherited translation in the first two والاعتبار لها clauses. Facsimile p76 confirms the wording and the explicitly negative third parallel.",
        "Full authorial argument compared; the large footnote begins below the printed rule and belongs to the modern editorial apparatus. No body text is lost at the p76/77 transition."

    {
      "page": 78,
      "entry_id": "MSH-066",
      "old_english": "Lest the foregoing suggest that the cognition that “arises” is newly produced because it comes later than that from which it arises, he removes the misunderstanding: “arising” here does not mean temporal origination, which is impossible in the Real's Essence and inseparable attributes, knowledge among them. [The phrase concerning disembodiment as a relation, discussed in philosophical science, is obscure in the consulted reading.] What appears as origination in attributes connected with His name *the Manifest* is, in respect of existence, appearance following hiddenness; in respect of the fixed entities, it is described as being preceded by nonexistence. Posteriority in cognition is therefore only posterior **in rank**, by way of natural priority: the later requires the earlier, yet the earlier is not thereby the efficient cause of the later. Divine attributes are not caused by anything, for efficient causation concerns originated things. All these cognitions are eternal and everlasting in one invariant mode; ignorance of none of them came first. Their realities possess a natural order, however, and knowledge relates to each according to its reality. This is why we say God's knowledge of temporal events is eternal, although it relates to them as they are: He knows the past as past, the present as present, and the future as future, without any alteration in His knowledge. The relation between knowledge and its object has no independent existence; therefore allowing for such a consideration in divine knowledge poses no difficulty. Understand.\n\nHe [Qūnawī] said, may God be pleased with him: “[What their realities entail is of two kinds. The first is their being cognized insofar as their multiplicity is absorbed in the Real's unity: the cognition of the differentiated within the undifferentiated. It is like a knowing intellect's discerning, with the eye of knowledge, what one seed potentially contains of branches, leaves, and fruit, and in each individual fruit what was contained in the first seed, and so on without end.]”\n\nSince knowledge relates to realities according to their requirements, they are sometimes apprehended together in one mode and sometimes as ordered. Their requirements have two modalities, since the unitary Essence and the realities each mirror the other. The first, in which the Essence mirrors the realities and they remain in one mode within It, is their cognition insofar as their multiplicity is absorbed in the unity of the Real: they do not appear in It as really distinguished, although they are present potentially. Their articulation is by consideration in relation to what will come afterward. This is the witnessing of the differentiated within the undifferentiated, in which the whole is contained within that perfection. But the perfection that embraces those realities is not complete [in the respect of manifestation] until existence becomes manifest in them and to them. The fixed entities, considered as such, remain nonexistent and never become manifest as fixed entities; nevertheless the Real beholds them with a knowledge-witnessing, not as independently existent objects of direct external witnessing. The names demand both perfections. Hence multiplicity here is by consideration, while unity is real—just as a seed includes the tree, its fruit, and the seeds within its fruit. The seed's unity is like the reality, and the multiplicity within it exists by consideration. Only—[sentence continues on p. 79].",
      "new_english": "Lest the foregoing suggest that the cognition that “arises” is newly produced because it comes later than that from which it arises, he removes the misunderstanding: “arising” here does not mean temporal origination, which is impossible in the Real's Essence and inseparable attributes, knowledge among them. “For abstraction is a relation, as explained in philosophy.” [The function of this printed/transcribed clause in the argument is uncertain.] What appears as origination in attributes connected with His name *the Manifest* is, in respect of existence, appearance following hiddenness; in respect of the fixed entities, it is described as being preceded by nonexistence. Posteriority in cognition is therefore only posterior **in rank**, by way of natural priority: the later requires the earlier, yet the earlier is not thereby the efficient cause of the later. Divine attributes are not caused by anything, for efficient causation concerns originated things. All these cognitions are eternal and everlasting in one invariant mode; ignorance of none of them came first. Their realities possess a natural order, however, and knowledge relates to each according to its reality. This is why we say God's knowledge of temporal events is eternal, although it relates to them as they are: He knows the past as past, the present as present, and the future as future, without any alteration in His knowledge. What changes is the relation between knowledge and its object, a relation that has no existence; therefore allowing for such a consideration in divine knowledge poses no difficulty. Understand.\n\nHe [Qūnawī] said, may God be pleased with him: “[What their realities entail is of two kinds. The first is their being cognized insofar as their multiplicity is absorbed in the Real's unity: the cognition of the differentiated within the undifferentiated. It is like a knowing intellect's discerning, with the eye of knowledge, what one seed potentially contains of branches, leaves, and fruit, and in each individual fruit what was contained in the first seed, and so on without end.]”\n\nSince knowledge relates to realities according to their requirements, they are sometimes apprehended together in one mode and sometimes as ordered. Their requirements have two modalities, since the unitary Essence and the realities each mirror the other. The first, in which the Essence mirrors the realities and they remain in one mode within It, is their cognition insofar as their multiplicity is absorbed in the unity of the Real: they do not appear in It as really distinguished, although they are present potentially. Their articulation is by consideration in relation to what will come afterward. This is the witnessing of the differentiated within the undifferentiated, in which the whole is contained within that perfection. But the perfection that embraces those realities is not complete [in the respect of manifestation] until existence becomes manifest in them and to them. The fixed entities, considered as such, remain nonexistent and never become manifest as fixed entities; nevertheless the Real beholds them by witnessing in knowledge, not by concrete witnessing (*shuhūd ʿaynī*). The names demand both perfections. Hence multiplicity here is by consideration, while unity is real—just as a seed includes the tree, its fruit, and the seeds within its fruit. The seed's unity is like the reality, and the multiplicity within it exists by consideration. Only—[sentence continues on p. 79].",
      "reasons": [
