    {
      "page": 79,
      "entry_id": "MSH-067",
      "old_english": "... the multiplicity latent in it knows that multiplicity truly; its knowledge does not change when the multiplicity comes to exist actually outside the mind. No perfection previously absent is thereby added to knowledge. Rather, the very same perfection acquires the attribute of external manifestation, so that the perfection proper to external existence may be obtained. The knower receives no increment beyond what was known at first; nevertheless, because what was known has now appeared externally, knowledge must relate to it as external so as to correspond to the eternal knowledge. Understand.\n\n**Qūnawī:** “The other mode is to conceive the rulings of unity group after group. Each group is conceived with the quiddities it contains, which are the forms of those multiple intellections by which the one existence is made to appear multiple. This is the reverse of the first absorption mentioned: there multiplicity was absorbed in unity; here unity is absorbed in multiplicity. Know this.”\n\nThe other mode required by the realities is that the realities themselves become mirrors of the Real. Their intelligible ordering then appears, because the judgements or descriptions of the one existence are conceived insofar as it appears in these realities, although those descriptions also belonged to it in hiddenness. These judgements are conceived group by group according to natural order, even though the whole collection can be conceived at once when considered simply as divine determinations. Their order follows the order of their externally manifested quiddities. Each group is conceived together with its quiddities, which are the forms of those intellections: loci for judgements first conceived all at once and then considered repeatedly through many manifestations. Al-Mahāʾimī specifies *external* quiddities because mental quiddities have no such sequential order of apprehension except insofar as they represent external things with an ordered manifestation.\n\nThese forms, namely external quiddities, are genuinely multiple outside the mind. They make the one existence appearing within them numerically multiple *with respect to its appearances*, not as it is in itself, because those forms are many mirrors of it and its reflected forms multiply with their multiplicity. The “absorption of unity”—its hiddenness within determinate realities—is the reverse of the first absorption, in which the multiplicity of realities is absorbed in existence. This is the witnessing of the comprehensive in the detailed. There is order in this witnessing according to the times at which existence appears in each locus. Multiplicity and temporal order belong intrinsically to the external quiddities, and to mental quiddities insofar as they are capable of external realization. Unity belongs to the Real with respect to what is in the Real. Understand.",

    {
      "page": 80,
      "entry_id": "MSH-068",
      "old_english": "**Second text. Qūnawī:** “Among the texts: know that the Real, insofar as it is unrestricted and all-encompassing, is not named by a name, assigned a judgement, or determined by a description or defining mark. Ascribing demand [*iqtiḍāʾ*] to it has no greater priority than ascribing non-demand, for a demand conceived or denied at that level is itself a determinate judgement and a restricted qualification.”\n\nHaving completed the discussion of unrestrictedness that is not opposed to restriction and is not confined to either member of that pair, to their conjunction, or to separateness from them, Qūnawī turns to unrestrictedness *as opposed to* restriction. This is the unrestrictedness expressed in the consideration before the first determination, and it may be considered both before and after that determination. It is still characterized through the concepts of unrestrictedness and universality, as indicated by “its comprehensiveness.” Yet it cannot be given any special name, or else it would cease to be unrestricted; nor may a special judgement be attributed, such as saying that it demands fixed entities or names or does not demand them, because either exclusive description opposes its universality.\n\nNor is the Real determined here by an attribute such as knowledge or by a distinguishing mark such as existence or life. Therefore the ascription of an intelligibly determinate demand for names or entities is no more appropriate than that of its denial. The qualification “intelligibly conceived” matters: these possibilities are contained within the first meaning of unrestrictedness and differ from it only under a consideration. What cannot apply at the present standpoint is *demand or non-demand conceived as a distinct judgement*, not a denial that the actuality corresponding to it may be found at another rank. Thus either affirmed demand or its denial would count as a determinate judgement.\n\nOne can express it as “demanding” or “not demanding” and describe the Essence as possessing or lacking a demand; but then the particular unrestrictedness opposed to restriction would no longer remain. Demand cannot be conceived as such under the exclusion just discussed, though determination comes in an order related to it. Rather, intelligible demand depends on the scientific or knowledge-determination, and that first knowledge-determination is not brought about as a consequence of the demand: it is already embraced within unrestrictedness in its primary sense. Understand.\n\n**Qūnawī:** “Know further that, although demand is intrinsic, it has three ranks. At the first rank it depends on neither a condition nor a necessitating factor producing its determination. At the second its determination depends on one condition only. At the third the manifestation of its effects depends on conditions, causes and mediators.” Al-Mahāʾimī begins to explain that neither the attribution of demand nor non-demand has priority in essential unrestrictedness ...       "page": 83,
      "entry_id": "MSH-071",
      "old_english": "... in its reality, but it differs according to its ranks, like the originating principle. It has three ranks ordered in its own source and two modes in its descent; at each rank a particular effect or several effects are manifested and determined. At the first there is the First Intellect; at the others, the effects already discussed. Qūnawī says both “appear” and “become determined” because the effects are concealed within the Essence and as yet indistinguishable; through manifestation they become distinguishable and determinate.\n\nThe universal effusion is general existence (*al-wujūd al-ʿāmm*). Al-Mahāʾimī suggests that this subtle approach can reconcile philosophers, who hold that only one proceeds from the One, with theologians, who assign all things directly to God without mediation; hence Qūnawī's admonition, “Understand.” Alternatively, one may say that the effusion is one but becomes manifold with ranks, while causes do not independently produce their effects but assign the conditions or times at which they appear. God knows best.\n\n**Third text. Qūnawī:** “One of the divine texts is that intrinsic, unitary knowledge is attributed multiplicity in respect of its relation to known things. Those things are apprehended only in respect of its determinations and relations.”\n\nHaving finished unrestrictedness considered as opposed to restriction, al-Mahāʾimī says Qūnawī begins the first delimitation, that of knowledge, because knowledge is the first relation. He calls this a divine text insofar as knowledge is the origin of divine names; the names together with the Essence constitute the Presence of divinity. Knowledge is termed “unitary” because it is one in the Presence of *aḥadiyya*, and “intrinsic” because it is not distinct from the Essence.\n\nIts further ruling is that multiplicity is attributed to unitary knowledge insofar as it relates to many known things, namely the fixed entities, the realities of possibilities. In the same way, multiplicity is attributed to unrestricted, one existence by considering its appearance in numerous loci, and to demand or effusion in relation to distinct recipients, even though these remain one at their source. Intrinsic knowledge is one and encompasses everything just as the Essence encompasses it. But considered solely in relation to the Essence, it is undifferentiated or comprehensive. The many things known are apprehended in detail only through knowledge's determinations by those things, that is, through its relations to them.\n\nHence the fixed entities are called “forms of knowledge” and “unmade.” It would be wrong to imagine that many forms are engraved into knowledge considered as a single intrinsic reality; rather, they are imprinted under the consideration of its many determinations, arising from its relations to the entities. Those determinations are mirrors for the fixed entities. **Qūnawī:** “Its relation to each known thing follows the known thing in the condition it has in itself, whether the known thing is simple or composite, temporal or spatial, or neither temporal nor spatial, bounded ...”",

      "entry_id": "MSH-072",
      "old_english": "**Qūnawī (continuing):** “... in receptivity and limited in its ruling and attribute, or without a limit and unlimited in the respects we have mentioned. Know this.”\n\nThis clarifies the universality of knowledge and its encompassing everything, although no new coming-to-be or change occurs within its original unity, even when such changes occur in its relations. Knowledge's relation to each known thing follows that thing. Each known thing proceeds from the one knowledge considered in its unity; nevertheless, because knowledge's determinations concern those things, each determination follows the nature of what determines it. Thus the *relation* takes on the character of the object, while the intrinsic knowledge, which underlies the relation, stays as it is. Such characters include simplicity or composition, temporality or atemporality, spatiality or non-spatiality, eternity or its absence.\n\nThe example of a simple, temporal, spatial and bounded object is a spoken letter of the alphabet; of a simple object outside such conditions, the intellects and souls; of a composite temporal-spatial object, things generated in the sublunary world; of a composite not situated in time and space, the sphere delimiting directions [according to the author's cosmology]. Knowledge's relations receive the characteristics without intrinsic knowledge receiving them. For example, someone knows that Zayd performs an action at a specified time. Beforehand he knows that Zayd *will* do it, and at the time knows he *is* doing it. A new temporal relation appears with Zayd's action, while the knowledge that Zayd acts at that time remains one and unchanged. Similarly, a composite is known as one in its totality, but in detailed consideration its intelligibility may require prior apprehension of the parts.       "new_english": "**Qūnawī (continuing):** “... in receptivity and limited in its ruling and attribute, or not temporally limited and infinite in the respects we have mentioned. Since the known thing determines the relation of knowledge, that relation follows its object.       "old_english": "A further point remains: the relation of the judge's ruling also depends on the judge's state.       "old_english": "... the Real and all existents. The third text showed that knowledge's determinations correspond to the determinations of known things. It follows that knowledge accompanies existence: since the first determination is the most comprehensive, its concomitants extend through the more particular determinations, because whatever necessarily accompanies the general also accompanies each particular falling under it, and a concomitant of a concomitant is likewise necessary. The mediation of the Intellect is grounded in spiritual affinity, for an agent and recipient must share a relevant affinity; hence the Intellect pours forth upon every spirit according to that spirit's preparedness.\n\nSpirit is immaterial; and, as philosophy demonstrates in this account, every immaterial reality is knowing. Knowledge must relate to the known thing, which is existence itself in reality, though it is other under a certain consideration. Accordingly, the Real knows, through one knowledge, its Essence, its attributes and infinitely many things.\n\nThus knowledge is a concomitant of existence with equal extension. The phrase “follows” means inseparable accompaniment. All things therefore, in the sense intended here, know God, hear His command and obey Him, as illustrated by transmitted accounts of stones and earth bearing witness to the call to prayer. Powers are principles of effects, and whatever acts must in some sense know what it brings about. God says, “Does He who created not know? He is the Subtle, the All-Aware” (Q 67:14). Hence even human limbs are aware, in their fashion, of what they do and of the heart to which they are joined, although they have neither speech nor imagination. Understand.\n\n**Qūnawī:** “The variation of knowledge follows the variation in how fully or deficiently a quiddity receives existence.       "old_english": "[Continuation from p. 88.] ... and, thirdly, what the ultimate scope of this relation is.\n\n**Qūnawī:** “Although I have indicated something of this in certain places in my books, within another matter and in its idiom, nevertheless, since I have devoted this book specifically to the *nuṣūṣ* belonging to the distinctive tastes of the station of perfection—not to the more general discourse of restricted tastes experienced by possessors of particular stations, which derive primarily from the presence of one divine name or attribute, the place of origin and spring of that particular taste—I must isolate and distinguish what pertains to the taste of the most perfect, most comprehensive station.       "old_english": "... things, or by considering, sensing, and imagining intermediate objects such as geometrical figures. It follows that nothing can be known in complete perfection because knowing every thing requires knowing the Real, and knowing the Real requires knowing His unrestrictedness. Ibn ʿArabī accordingly says [verse]: “I do not know the reality of any thing; how could I know it when You are within it?” This argument establishes why one cannot know God as He knows Himself: divine knowing is not the impression of a representation of the known requiring further knowledge of its background, but His own reality being present to Him. This latter claim calls for philosophical demonstration.\n\nThe printed commentary next attributes to “Shaykh Ibn ʿArabī” the saying that there is another, unveiled way of knowing this impossibility, which may not be written down. [The wording also occurs in the Qūnawī lemma on p91; the printed attribution is retained rather than silently reassigned.] The previous words provide only a hint. Al-Mahāʾimī tentatively suggests that what we know of the Real is always His outward aspect, never the Reality as He knows it, which is present to none but Him. Describing this without qualification could wrongly suggest that God Himself knows only an outward surface. Since outwardness and inwardness are relative to *us*, that limitation does not apply to God. God knows best.\n\n**Qūnawī:** “This remains so even if the taste, knowledge acquired by its possessor, and witnessing rest on the presence of a divine name that constitutes the *qibla* of that station, and the end of his knowledge of the Real is reached there—especially insofar as the name is identical with the Named, as we have explained elsewhere. But these are relative ends. Beginnings and ends are markers of relative perfections; the matter is otherwise with respect to true perfection. God alludes to this in speaking to the most perfect of His servants: ‘And to your Lord is the final end’ [Q 53:42].”\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This judgement—that the Real, and indeed anything, cannot be known with full knowledge—applies even when taste, meaning immediate experience; the knowledge attained by its possessor, meaning direct knowledge (*ʿilm ʿaynī*); and witnessing, meaning the eye of certainty thereby attained, are referred, together with the resulting station, to the presence of a name among the divine names. He considers this attribution ... [continued on p. 94].       "old_en": "**Text Eleven — Qūnawī:** “A clear text and universal rule by which one learns the meaning of divine responsiveness and answer, and of their refusal.”\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** After dividing receptive capacities, Qūnawī asks which requests are answered and which are not. The subsequent mention of refusal makes clear that the image cannot be read as making God literally obedient to a creature. It is meant to stress the elevated standing of a servant who obeys God wholeheartedly and whose petition is, by divine gift, especially responsive. Qūnawī calls the principle “clear” and “universal” to present it as a rule that can be examined against the varied experience of answered requests. “Conveying knowledge” of the rule stresses that knowledge follows from it as a consequence; refusal is mentioned because a thing is often better grasped through its contrary.\n\n**Qūnawī:** “Know that the complete, explicit measure and the truly verified, sound proof drawn from taste—by which one knows when the servant is obedient to his Lord and when the divine answer reaches him swiftly in the very matter he asks, without obstacle or delay—is sound knowledge and perfect responsiveness. The more correct his knowledge of the Real and his conception of Him, the swifter the answer in exactly what he asks. The more complete his attentiveness to the Real's commands and the greater his readiness to act upon them with perfect obedience, the more complete is the Real's responsive accommodation of him compared with His accommodation of other servants.”\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** A “measure” ordinarily establishes heaviness and lightness; a “proof” establishes a conclusion through inferential form. Both are transferred metaphorically to an experiential rule. “Complete” and “explicit” deny an undisclosed defect or ambiguity in the rule, and “sound” guards against a seemingly rigorous but fallacious argument. The repeated qualifications respond to the common impression that, because many people pray while fewer receive the very things requested, no reliable principle of response can be identified.       "new_en": "**Text Eleven — Qūnawī:** “A clear text and universal rule yielding knowledge of divine responsiveness and answer, and of their refusal.”\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Having finished discussing those who receive, he begins to discuss which of them are answered and which are not. Since answering resembles carrying out a command, because supplication and command resemble one another in their verbal form, he calls answering “responsiveness” (*muṭāwaʿa*) by an explicit metaphor. It means apprehending His presence in the things witnessed without confinement, **indwelling (*ḥulūl*) or union (*ittiḥād*)**. Attentiveness to divine commands includes explicit words and intimations, acting on strict obligations and taking appropriate care with prohibitions, whose observance is a commanded abstention. One who hastens to carry these out achieves fuller human obedience; the corresponding “divine compliance” is, as already stated, a metaphor and should not be compared to obedience imposed upon a subordinate.",
      "new_en": "Since the expression here contains some ambiguity, he elaborates it: “the more correct his knowledge of the Real.” Since “knowledge” is most often used for intellectual apprehension, he explains it by adding “and the more correct his conception of Him.” He uses both expressions so that “conception” will not suggest that God has a form within which He is confined. The divine answer in the very thing asked is then swifter. This comes through seeing Him in everything without confinement, indwelling in things, or union with them. “More complete attentiveness to the Real's commands” means attending to His explicit expressions and indications, adopting the more cautious courses and the strict prescriptions. Prohibitions are included, since abstaining from prohibited things is commanded. Hastening to carry them out in action, with perfect obedience and complete exertion, makes the Real's responsiveness to him more complete than His responsiveness to other servants—even if those others are His enemies, to whom the Real is not responsive at all.",
      "reason": "Restore omitted contrast with other servants/enemies and precise al-ahwat/al-aza'im, remove added doctrinal explanation absent from this pair."
    },
    {
      "id": "MSH-P133",
      "pair_sequence": 1,
      "old_en": "**Qūnawī (continuing Text Eleven):** “... because of their perfect obedience, sound knowledge of God and accurate conception of Him. The saying ‘Call upon Me and I will answer you’ (Q 40:60) alludes to this. One who lacks correct, witnessing-based knowledge and an adequate conception is not really calling upon the Real to whom the promise of answer is addressed. Rather, in supplication he turns toward individualized images formed in his mind from his own reasoning and imagination, from another person's imagination and reasoning, or from their combination.”",
      "new_en": "**Qūnawī (continuing Text Eleven):** “... because of their perfect obedience, sound knowledge of God and accurate conception of Him. The saying ‘Call upon Me and I will answer you’ (Q 40:60) alludes to this. One who lacks sound witnessing knowledge and whose conception is relative is not calling upon the Real who has guaranteed him an answer by saying, ‘Call upon Me and I will answer you’ (Q 40:60). Rather, in supplication he turns toward individualized images formed in his mind from his own reasoning and imagination, from another person's imagination and reasoning, or from their combination.”",
      "reason": "Translate النسبي التصور as relative conception, and correct the agency: the Real gives the promise; He is not the one to whom it is addressed."
    },
    {
      "id": "MSH-P133",
      "pair_sequence": 2,
      "old_en": "**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Such a person may be deprived of the answer in exactly the matter asked, or experience a delay. Qūnawī adduces both experiential observation and a Qurʾānic verse. He carefully says that *most* prayers of the great spiritual masters are answered; he does not claim an exhaustive induction showing that every one is. Al-Mahāʾimī explicitly labels this an inference from incomplete induction (*istiqrāʾ nāqiṣ*), whose evidentiary weight is correspondingly limited. Such masters join proper knowledge with the more exacting quality of obedience. The repeated mention of conception prevents “knowledge” from being understood as cognition of the divine only under attributes, without right orientation to the Real.",
      "new_en": "**Al-Mahāʾimī:** For this reason someone in this condition is deprived of an answer in the very thing he requested, or it—that is, the answer—is delayed. He argues for the stated rule first from what occurs and then from the Qurʾānic text: because perfect knowledge brings about answering and perfect obedience brings about responsiveness, the state of the great ones among God's people entails that most of their supplications are answered.",
      "reason": "Restore the actual scope of pair2; move its previously imported discussion of incomplete induction to pair3, where it belongs."
    },
    {
      "id": "MSH-P133",
      "pair_sequence": 3,
      "old_en": "Because incomplete induction cannot establish the universal rule conclusively, the commentary reads Q 40:60 as its scriptural basis. It understands the verse as a promise to the one who truly addresses the Real, and uses the opposite implication (*mafḥūm al-mukhālafa*) to argue that one who instead addresses a mental image need not receive the *specific* response thus promised. Correct witnessing consists in apprehending the Real in all things without confining Him in them, making Him indwell them, or identifying Him through union with them. The verse is repeated to distinguish these kinds of petition from the petition of the desperate, who may be answered in virtue of their necessity even without this cultivated knowledge. That second case continues on p. 134.",
      "new_en": "He uses “most” because that is what is known with certainty. It has not been established by complete induction that all their supplications are answered, which would allow an argument by complete induction; rather, the argument is from incomplete induction. He then indicates the ground of the argument by saying “because of perfect responsiveness,” together with knowledge of God and conception of Him: they combine the condition of answering with the conditions of responsiveness, which exceed answering. How, then, could answering fail to occur for them? He gives responsiveness priority here to indicate that the perfection of knowledge is completed only through it. He repeats “and conception” so that “knowledge” will not be taken to mean merely apprehending Him from the standpoint of His attributes, as the term might suggest.",
      "reason": "Restore the Arabic paragraph on incomplete induction and its causal explanation; remove material belonging to pair4."
    },
    {
      "id": "MSH-P133",
      "pair_sequence": 4,
      "old_en": "[The online transcription places a lengthy modern editorial footnote on conditions and times of supplication after marker (1). It is excluded.]",
      "new_en": "Since an argument from incomplete induction gives incomplete indication, he adduces the Qurʾānic text: “Call upon Me and I will answer you” (Q 40:60). Its explicit wording indicates that when someone turns toward Him with a correct conception, the Real answers without another condition. By its contrary implication it indicates that one lacking sound knowledge—that is, witnessing knowledge through which the Real is witnessed in everything without being confined to things, indwelling in them, or united with them—is not calling upon the Real, and so the answer guaranteed by “Call upon Me and I will answer you” is not necessarily due to him. He repeats the verse because the desperately distressed person may be answered ... [the sentence continues on p.134].",
      "reason": "Replace an editorial-footnote notice incorrectly standing in place of the medieval main-text paragraph; restore Qur'anic argument, its negations, and page-boundary continuation."
    },
    {
      "id": "MSH-P134",
      "pair_sequence": 1,
      "old_en": "**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The separate promise of answer to the desperate—“Who answers the distressed one when he calls?” (Q 27:62)—is conditioned by necessity (*iḍṭirār*), not simply by the quality of deliberative knowledge that governs the preceding class. A petitioner lacking adequate knowledge may turn toward a mentally individuated picture. Since such a picture cannot correspond to the unrestricted Real without remainder, the image as such does not guarantee an unqualified answer.\n\nThe mental picture may result from one's intellectual reasoning, one's own imagination, the imagination or speculation of another person, or a mixture of these. In speaking of a person's own faculties Qūnawī puts rational examination first, since a seeker should ask whether a proposed account is fitting. In describing borrowed accounts, he reverses the order to signal the danger of conforming one's mental image to another's imagination before examining the reasoning behind it. A corrupt image can become entrenched when private imagining and borrowed conception reinforce one another. The point is to avoid directing worship toward one's own limited image while thinking that image exhausts divine reality.\n\nSomeone in that state may not receive the *particular* thing requested, although the matter may be answered in a different way according to whatever partial aspect of the divine names the petitioner actually apprehends. Thus an answer in some respect is not ruled out; Qūnawī's restriction concerns the very object of the petition. His added clarification “that is, the answer” prevents the reader from overlooking this distinction.\n\n**Qūnawī (continuing to p. 135):** “When such a person is answered, this is because of the secret of divine accompaniment, according to which nothing is devoid ...”\n\n[The remaining lines of the web transcription on this printed page, beginning «يسأل عنه وإذا كان مستبشرا», belong to a lengthy modern editor's *hāmish*, not to al-Mahāʾimī; they are deliberately omitted from the running Arabic text.]",
      "new_en": "**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The separate promise of answer to the desperate—“Who answers the distressed one when he calls?” (Q 27:62)—is conditioned by desperate necessity (*iḍṭirār*), rather than by supplication itself as in the preceding case. A petitioner lacking adequate knowledge may turn toward a mentally individuated picture. Since that image necessarily fails to correspond to the Real, it does not unconditionally necessitate an answer.\n\nThe mental picture may result from one's intellectual reasoning, one's own imagination, the imagination or speculation of another person, or a mixture of these. In speaking of a person's own faculties Qūnawī puts rational examination first, since a seeker should ask whether a proposed account is fitting. In describing borrowed accounts, he reverses the order to signal the danger of conforming one's mental image to another's imagination before examining the reasoning behind it. A corrupt image can become entrenched when private imagining and borrowed conception reinforce one another. He describes these corrupt images so that they may be avoided in every case.\n\nSomeone in that state may not receive the *particular* thing requested, although the matter may be answered in a different way according to whatever partial aspect of the divine names the petitioner actually apprehends. Thus an answer in some respect is not ruled out; Qūnawī's restriction concerns the very object of the petition. His clarification “that is, the answer” prevents the delay from being understood as referring only to an answer in exactly what was requested. The wording implies that the person is not without some answer, because he calls upon the Real under one of His aspects.\n\n**Qūnawī (continuing to p. 135):** “When such a person is answered, this is because of the secret of divine accompaniment, according to which nothing is devoid ...”\n\n[The remaining lines of the web transcription on this printed page, beginning «يسأل عنه وإذا كان مستبشرا», belong to a lengthy modern editor's *hāmish*, not to al-Mahāʾimī; they are deliberately omitted from the running Arabic text.]",
      "reason": "Correct explicit contrast: لا بنفس الدعاء كهذه concerns supplication itself, not deliberative knowledge. Remove the added qualification 'without remainder'; preserve the commentary's assertion about the deficient mental image in this case. Remove an interpretive expansion absent from the supplied Arabic. Restore explicit role of pronoun clarification and final causal statement."
    },
    {
      "id": "MSH-P135",
      "pair_sequence": 1,
      "old_en": "**Qūnawī (completion of p. 134):** “... of the Real, or else because of the perfect concentration arising in desperate people, who have been promised an answer in consequence of their plea born of necessity and the preparedness produced by that very necessity.”\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** If a person focused on a limited mental picture nevertheless receives the particular answer without delay, one of two accounts applies. First, divine accompaniment (*maʿiyya*) reaches throughout beings: the relations and appearances of the divine attributes embrace every cosmic reality and form, as indicated by “He is with you wherever you are” (Q 57:4). The commentator carefully says “divine” accompaniment rather than identifying it simply with the unrestricted Essence in itself. The Essence, considered as absolutely independent of all worlds, has no relational dependence on things. “Withness” is described under the attributes; the accompanying Qurʾānic reference to divine seeing qualifies a reading of identity or presence as crude spatial occupation.\n\nEven this accompaniment does not automatically necessitate the very thing prayed for: the petitioner may be attending to the image under one aspect as a locus of manifestation, or under another aspect as somehow identical with the Real. The image therefore has two possible respects in which an answer may be enabled or obstructed; which predominates depends on further conditions.\n\nSecond, a desperate person's complete concentration of aspiration (*jamʿiyyat al-himma*) generates the receptivity attached to the promise of Q 27:62. Even if his conceptual orientation is deficient, necessity may draw his whole attention toward the One who answers, since the Real's accompaniment is not absent even from the concept by which he calls. The decisively relevant readiness comes from the existential condition of distress, not merely from the spoken wording of the request. The pronoun in “produced by it” refers, al-Mahāʾimī specifies, to necessity rather than the act of requesting.\n\n**Qūnawī:** “The state of someone like this differs from that of one possessing a right conception and a verified knowledge. The latter has the Real present to awareness and turns toward Him with a genuine presence and orientation. Though this may not be comprehensive in every aspect, it is enough that he truly conceives and recalls the Real in directing himself, even at some ranks and from the aspect of certain names and attributes. This is the state of the intermediates among God's people, and their state ...”",
      "new_en": "**Qūnawī (completion of p. 134):** “... of the Real, or else because of the perfect concentration arising in desperate people, who have been promised an answer in consequence of their plea born of necessity and the preparedness produced by that very necessity.”\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** If a person focused on a limited mental picture nevertheless receives the particular answer without delay, one of two accounts applies. First, divine accompaniment (*maʿiyya*) reaches throughout beings: the relations and appearances of the divine attributes embrace every cosmic reality and form, as indicated by “He is with you wherever you are” (Q 57:4). The commentator carefully says “divine” accompaniment rather than identifying it simply with the unrestricted Essence in itself. The Essence as such, being independent of all worlds, has no relation to things as such. The term “divine” indicates that the relation is considered under the attributes. Although ‘He is with you’ might suggest an essential accompaniment of identity, that suggestion is removed by ‘God sees what you do.’\n\nThis pervasive accompaniment is a cause of answering, because it entails that nothing is devoid of the Real [the supplied Arabic at this point is defective]. It is nevertheless not a cause that necessitates answering, because the petitioner attends to the image as the Real Himself rather than as a locus of manifestation. The image has two aspects: one calls for answering and the other prevents it. If the former is strengthened by some hidden factor, the person is answered; otherwise not.\n\nSecond, a desperate person's complete concentration of aspiration (*jamʿiyyat al-himma*) generates the receptivity attached to the promise of Q 27:62. Even if his conceptual orientation is deficient, necessity may draw his whole attention toward the One who answers, since the Real's accompaniment is not absent even from the concept by which he calls. The request born of necessity gives the divine accompaniment preponderance, together with the preparedness arising from that necessity as a locus of mercy [the supplied connecting syntax is unclear]. The pronoun in “produced by it” refers, al-Mahāʾimī specifies, to necessity rather than the act of requesting. This second cause necessitates answering; understand this.\n\n**Qūnawī:** “The state of someone like this differs from that of one possessing a right conception and a verified knowledge. The latter has the Real present to awareness and turns toward Him with a genuine presence and orientation. Though this may not be comprehensive in every aspect, it is enough that he truly conceives and recalls the Real in directing himself, even at some ranks and from the aspect of certain names and attributes. This is the state of the intermediates among God's people, and their state ...”",
      "reason": "Translate the claimed absence of relation, not merely absence of dependence; replace unsupported spatial-occupation explanation with the commentary's explicit distinction. Restore fixed attribution of the petitioner's error and the distinct enabling/obstructing aspects; flag the corrupted خلق/الخلق phrase rather than silently treating it as established text. Restore the comparative predominance and mercy language instead of importing a spoken-versus-unspoken contrast. Restore the concluding contrast between a cause that permits and a cause that necessitates answering."
    },
    {
      "id": "MSH-P136",
      "pair_sequence": 2,
      "old_en": "**Al-Mahāʾimī:** A person who addresses a mental form, even if occasionally answered in exactly what he asks, differs from a person possessing correct conception and verified knowledge. Correct conception is defined by correspondence to reality, not by a merely stipulated limit, and should have decisive warrant—either intellectual or experiential. The knowledgeable recipient brings the Real to awareness before petitioning and orients himself toward Him with genuine presence, so that the Qurʾānic promise “Call upon Me; I will answer you” (Q 40:60) applies under its proper meaning. This contrasts with supplication directed to an imagined figure.",
      "new_en": "**Al-Mahāʾimī:** A person who addresses a mental form, even if occasionally answered in exactly what he asks, differs from a person possessing correct conception and verified knowledge. Correct conception is defined by correspondence to reality, not by a merely stipulated limit, and must be accompanied by decisive proof—either intellectual or experiential. The knowledgeable recipient brings the Real to awareness before petitioning and orients himself toward Him with genuine presence, so that the Qurʾānic promise “Call upon Me; I will answer you” (Q 40:60) applies under its proper meaning. This contrasts with someone who brings an imagined form in his mind to awareness and turns toward it: there is no necessity at all that he be answered. The person with correct conception must be answered even if his conception does not extend to every aspect—the Essence, names, attributes, and all the remaining ranks and considerations. For the necessity of answering, it suffices that he have a conception corresponding to the Real at some ranks and bring the Real at those ranks to awareness as he turns toward Him.",
      "reason": "Restore the substantial final part of pair2 formerly displaced into pair3 and undertranslated. Preserve لا بدّ and الدليل القطعي without weakening necessity into recommendation."
    },
    {
      "id": "MSH-P136",
      "pair_sequence": 3,
      "old_en": "The correct conception need not encompass the Essence, every divine name and every rank. An authentic orientation under one determinate divine name or attribute may suffice. It is essential, however, to distinguish this from an imagined appearance regarded as a separate self-subsistent object. The former apprehends a real aspect of the divine order; the latter confines attention to a finite picture without understanding its status as manifestation. The qualified but genuine knowledge of certain divine names belongs to the *intermediate* spiritual rank. These recipients often obtain an exact response; however, response can still vary or be delayed in accordance with the governing power and boundaries of the particular name. The veiled, by contrast, have no unconditional right to the specified answer.",
      "new_en": "Since this could suggest that some veiled people also turn toward the Real at certain ranks, he explains that these are high ranks attained from the aspects of certain names and attributes, not from the aspect of the imagined form, which impairs knowledge. Bringing some divine ranks to awareness does not impair it. Conception at certain ranks of names and attributes is the state of the intermediates among God's people. Thus they are often answered in exactly what they ask without delay; if the answer is delayed or substituted, this is in accordance with the authority and restriction of that name. The state mentioned previously—bringing to awareness an imagined form in the mind—is the state of the veiled, for whom answering is not necessary at all. Such a person does not know that the form is one of the Real's loci of manifestation, but instead holds a mistaken conception of it [the supplied expression «يتوهم غيبتها», literally “imagines its absence,” is unclear], and so grows distant from the Real. The intermediate knows it to be of His names, thereby draws near to the Real, and must be answered. Understand this.",
      "reason": "Restore the Arabic pair's reasoning and distinguish name-conditioned cognition from the veiled person's misconception; do not invent self-subsistence as the translation of غيبتها."
    },
    {
      "id": "MSH-P137",
      "pair_sequence": 1,
      "old_en": "**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Qūnawī has distinguished the veiled, who may sometimes receive an answer because of an additional circumstance, from intermediate people who commonly receive what they ask through more accurate knowledge or more complete obedience. He now explains why the comprehensive person's apprehension is of a different order. Their petition follows the particular essential disclosure earlier called lightning-like (*barqī*), the receipt of which marks full realization of the station of perfection.\n\n**Crucial temporal distinction:** Although this disclosure itself does not persist for even two breaths, **its fruition is a comprehensive and abiding knowledge** of the aspects (*ḥaythiyyāt*) of all names and attributes, the divine and cosmic ranks, and their various considerations. Following the special disclosure, the accomplished knower descends to the ranks of names, attributes and other modes without losing the correct apprehension gained from seeing the Real without a locus. Because that initial witnessing was complete, its intelligible imprint remains in the spirit after the immediate disclosure disappears. Consequently no attribute veils the Essence from this recipient, nor does the Essence veil the attributes, nor do the other levels block one another. The new comprehensiveness is not a continuous uninterrupted repetition of the original “flash”; rather, the brief witnessing has enduring cognitive and spiritual effects. This directly connects pp. 108–110 with p. 137.\n\nIn this station the knower's petition draws on the combined languages of the Essence and divine names. Al-Mahāʾimī takes Qūnawī's denial of delay to imply that the requested object is not replaced either. The commentator's reason is that a true all-comprehending orientation does not suffer the incompleteness that arises from being governed by one restricted name alone.\n\n**Qūnawī:** “Furthermore the perfect ones, and whichever of the singular individuals God wills, have access to the Preserved Tablet, indeed to the Pen-rank, indeed to the Presence of divine knowledge. They therefore discern what is decreed to occur, because knowledge of its occurrence has preceded it and it must come about. Thus they ask for nothing whose existence is impossible because it has not been decreed, nor do their aspirations turn toward seeking or willing such a thing. I include ‘willing it’ because there are some whose volition conditions the occurrence of things even without supplicating or verbally asking the Real for their occurrence.”",
      "new_en": "**Al-Mahāʾimī:** Qūnawī has distinguished the veiled, who may sometimes receive an answer because of an additional circumstance, from intermediate people who commonly receive what they ask through more accurate knowledge or more complete obedience. He now explains why the comprehensive person's apprehension is of a different order. Their petition follows the particular essential disclosure earlier called lightning-like (*barqī*), the receipt of which marks full realization of the station of perfection.\n\n**Crucial temporal distinction:** Although this disclosure itself does not persist for even two breaths, **its fruition is a comprehensive and abiding knowledge** of the aspects (*ḥaythiyyāt*) of all names and attributes, the divine and cosmic ranks, and their various considerations. Following the special disclosure, the accomplished knower descends to the ranks of names, attributes and other modes without losing the correct apprehension gained from seeing the Real without a locus. Because that witnessing was complete, the conception remains in their spirits even after the disclosure ceases. Consequently no attribute veils the Essence from this recipient, nor does the Essence veil the attributes, nor do the other levels block one another. The wording ‘through the most complete witnessing’ indicates that the conception disappears only when witnessing is incomplete; where it is complete, the conception does not disappear.\n\nIn this station the knower's petition draws on the combined languages of the Essence and divine names. Al-Mahāʾimī takes Qūnawī's denial of delay to imply that the requested object is not replaced either. Changing the requested object is an even greater withholding of acceptance than delaying it. Delay is a kind of refusal, and there is no refusal when the request is made through the tongue of the Essence and the names—how much less when it is made through the tongues of them all.\n\n**Qūnawī:** “Furthermore the perfect ones, and whichever of the singular individuals God wills, have access to the Preserved Tablet, indeed to the Pen-rank, indeed to the Presence of divine knowledge. They therefore discern what is decreed to occur, because knowledge of its occurrence has preceded it and it must come about. Thus they ask for nothing whose existence is impossible because it has not been decreed, nor do their aspirations turn toward seeking or willing such a thing. I include ‘willing it’ because there are some whose volition conditions the occurrence of things even without supplicating or verbally asking the Real for their occurrence.”",
      "reason": "Translate التصور as the continuing conception, without adding the notion of an intelligible imprint. Replace editorial cross-reference and interpretive summary with the explicit explanation in the Arabic; existing editorial note retains the thematic cross-reference. Restore the two explicit arguments for no substitution/no delay, rather than substituting a generalized account of restricted names."
    },
    {
      "id": "MSH-P138",
      "pair_sequence": 1,
      "old_en": "**Qūnawī:** “I witnessed this concerning our master—may God sanctify his spirit—over many years, in more matters than I can enumerate. He told me that he saw the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, in one of his visionary events, and that the Prophet gave him glad tidings, saying: ‘God is quicker to answer you than you are to supplicate Him.’”\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This provides another explanation for the asserted immediacy of answers to the perfect ones. Among the poles (*aqṭāb*), the accomplished are said to have knowledge of divine will, and among certain singular individuals (*afrād*) of the more comprehensive willing or choice that precedes a particular determination. The commentary distinguishes degrees of awareness: the Preserved Tablet, identified with the Universal Soul and containing detailed inscriptions of cosmic events; the Pen-rank, identified with the First Intellect and expressing those inscriptions more comprehensively; and the Presence of divine knowledge on which both depend.\n\nBecause the people of essential disclosure descend through and know these ranks, they are said to discern what has been determined to occur. They therefore do not petition for a nonexistent outcome that divine knowledge has excluded. The impossibility in question is **not intrinsic impossibility**—it need not be a contradiction in the nature of the proposed event. Rather, a thing may be impossible *in relation to the determinate content of infallible prior divine knowledge*: its actual occurrence contrary to that knowledge would entail that divine knowledge had been false. Those with a share in knowledge of the decree do not direct will, aspiration or formal prayer toward what has been decisively excluded. Hence an apparent refusal in such a case does not arise.\n\nThe words about *willing* rather than merely *asking* matter because the causally relevant condition may, on this account, be an accomplished person's aspiration or will without verbal supplication. Al-Mahāʾimī then distinguishes what is **definitively fixed** in the divine decree (*jāzim*) from what is **conditioned or suspended** (*muʿallaq*). The latter is said to depend on supplication or other ordained causes, while the former does not depend on those additional conditions. If an event is divinely decreed to occur upon the will of such a person, it occurs with that will even if no explicit petition is voiced. This is a claim about the structure of a conditioned decree, not a claim of sovereign, self-subsisting creaturely creation.\n\n[Editorial distinction: a modern footnote identifies “our master” as Ibn ʿArabī. That identification is plausible for Qūnawī but has not been independently checked against a critical edition or manuscript. The footnote is excluded from the translated running text.]",
      "new_en": "**Qūnawī:** “I witnessed this concerning our master—may God sanctify his spirit—over many years, in more matters than I can enumerate. He told me that he saw the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, in one of his visionary events, and that the Prophet gave him glad tidings, saying: ‘God is quicker to answer you than you are to supplicate Him.’”\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** This provides another explanation for the asserted immediacy of answers to the perfect ones. Among the poles (*aqṭāb*), the accomplished are said to have knowledge of divine will, and among certain singular individuals (*afrād*) of the more comprehensive willing or choice that precedes a particular determination. The supplied explanation distinguishes the preceding, comprehensive willing (*mashīʾa*) from the particularizing will (*irāda*), although the construction explaining the singular individuals' exemption from the latter is difficult. The commentary then distinguishes degrees of awareness: the Preserved Tablet, identified with the Universal Soul and containing detailed inscriptions of cosmic events; the Pen-rank, identified with the First Intellect and containing those inscriptions in undifferentiated form; and the Presence of divine knowledge on which both depend.\n\nBecause the people of essential disclosure must descend through and pass through these ranks, they know their contents and discern what has been determined to occur and what has not. Qūnawī mentions only the first of these paired alternatives, as in the verse mentioning ‘garments that protect you from heat’ (Q 16:81), where one counterpart stands for the other as well. They therefore do not petition for a nonexistent outcome that divine knowledge has excluded. The impossibility in question is **not intrinsic impossibility**—it need not be a contradiction in the nature of the proposed event. Rather, a thing may be impossible *in relation to the determinate content of infallible prior divine knowledge*: its actual occurrence contrary to that knowledge would entail that divine knowledge had been false. Those with a share in knowledge of the decree do not direct will, aspiration or formal prayer toward what has been decisively excluded. Hence an apparent refusal in such a case does not arise.\n\nThe words about *willing* rather than merely *asking* matter because the causally relevant condition may, on this account, be an accomplished person's aspiration or will without verbal supplication. Al-Mahāʾimī then distinguishes what is **definitively fixed** in the divine decree (*jāzim*) from what is **conditioned or suspended** (*muʿallaq*). The latter is said to depend on supplication or other ordained causes, while the former does not depend on those additional conditions. If an event is divinely decreed to occur upon the will of such a person, it occurs with that will even if no explicit petition is voiced. \n\n[Editorial distinction: the modern footnote identifying “our master” as Ibn ʿArabī is excluded. Al-Mahāʾimī himself explicitly names Muḥyī al-Dīn ibn ʿArabī in the continuation on p.139; the attribution therefore does not depend solely on that modern footnote.]",
      "reason": "Make the difficult mashīʾa/irāda construction explicit rather than silently treating the existing smooth paraphrase as a settled reading. Translate إجمالا as undifferentiated, preserving its contrast with the Tablet's detailed inscriptions. Restore the omitted rhetorical comparison with Q16:81 and both alternatives of the decree. Remove an explanatory conclusion absent from the Arabic running text; the translation already preserves dependence on divine decree. Correct the evidential claim using the adjacent canonical Arabic on p139, which expressly names Ibn Arabi."
    },
    {
      "id": "MSH-P139",
      "pair_sequence": 1,
      "old_en": "**Al-Mahāʾimī:** In explaining “I witnessed,” he means that he gained from the perfected, perfecting master Muḥyī al-Dīn ibn ʿArabī—may God sanctify his spirit—knowledge resembling direct vision: Ibn ʿArabī had seen the Prophet, blessings and peace upon him, in one of his spiritual occurrences, that is, his unveilings or intimate conversations. The Prophet gave him the good news: “God is quicker in answering you than you are [in turning to Him].” That is, God responds through the mere will, before supplication is uttered. Qūnawī sets out the long expression about the vision, first to indicate whom Ibn ʿArabī saw, and then to extol it as prophetic glad tidings; he subsequently expounds what was compressed in the report while retaining its wording.\n\n**Qūnawī:** “This station is above the station in which prayers are answered. It is among the distinctive characteristics of perfect responsiveness (*kamāl al-muṭāwaʿa*), whose station is above ordinary responsiveness. Ordinary responsiveness is confined to what was indicated previously: promptly carrying out commands, pursuing what pleases the Real, and fulfilling His rights to the extent of one's ability. The Prophet alluded to this when his uncle Abū Ṭālib, seeing how quickly God answered his appeals, said, ‘How swiftly your Lord comes to what you desire, Muḥammad!’ Another report says, ‘How responsive your Lord is to you!’ The Prophet answered, ‘And you, uncle—if you obey Him, He will respond to you.’ The station I called higher than this concerns the servant's complete conformity, in virtue of his reality, to what the Real desires of him through the first, universal will, related to the attainment of complete *jalāʾ* and *istijlāʾ*. That is what calls forth the world's existentiation, together with the Perfect Human who is the intended entity in particular. Everything besides him is intended derivatively, for his sake and by reason of him: whatever is indispensable to attaining the intended end is itself intended. This is what I mean by ‘intended derivatively.’”\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The station at which mere willing is answered is higher than the station of verbally expressed prayers, since the latter requires the additional act of giving voice to the request before the answer. Response to willing is a characteristic of the servant's perfected responsiveness, through which the divine will responds to his will before he speaks. Perfect responsiveness is thus higher than simple responsiveness, wherein the divine response follows verbal petition. Ordinary responsiveness, as previously described, consists in hastening to [the duties whose detailed account continues on p. 140].",
      "new_en": "**Al-Mahāʾimī:** In explaining “I witnessed,” he means that he gained from the perfected, perfecting master Muḥyī al-Dīn ibn ʿArabī—may God sanctify his spirit—knowledge resembling direct vision: Ibn ʿArabī had seen the Prophet, blessings and peace upon him, in one of his spiritual occurrences, that is, his unveilings or intimate conversations. The Prophet gave him the good news: “God is quicker in answering you than you are [in turning to Him].” That is, God responds through the mere will, before supplication is uttered. Qūnawī gives the long account of seeing the Prophet and receiving the glad tidings, first to indicate that he saw one whose being seen is a seeing of the Real, then to praise the vision as glad tidings from the Prophet. He next explains what he had stated in summary while preserving the Prophet's reported wording.\n\n**Qūnawī:** “This station is above the station in which prayers are answered. Ordinary responsiveness is confined to what was indicated previously: promptly carrying out commands, pursuing what pleases the Real, and fulfilling His rights to the extent of one's ability. The Prophet alluded to this when his uncle Abū Ṭālib, seeing how quickly God answered his appeals, said, ‘How swiftly your Lord comes to what you desire, Muḥammad!’ Another report says, ‘How responsive your Lord is to you!’ The Prophet answered, ‘And you, uncle—if you obey Him, He will respond to you.’ The station I called higher than this concerns the servant's complete conformity, in virtue of his reality, to what the Real desires of him through the first, universal will, related to the attainment of complete *jalāʾ* and *istijlāʾ*. That is what calls forth the world's existentiation, together with the Perfect Human who is the intended entity in particular. Everything besides him is intended derivatively, for his sake and by reason of him: whatever is indispensable to attaining the intended end is itself intended. This is what I mean by ‘intended derivatively.’”\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The station at which mere willing is answered is higher than the station of verbally expressed prayers, since the latter requires the additional act of giving voice to the request before the answer.     {
      "id": "MSH-P140",
      "pair_sequence": 1,
      "old_en": "**Al-Mahāʾimī:** [The ordinary station entails] carrying out the Real's obligatory commands, pursuing His pleasure through recommended works, and observing His rights by holding correct belief concerning Him and acting sincerely, without seeking payment or self-interested advantage. Qūnawī restricts these activities to what lies within one's capacity, because their perfect accomplishment properly belongs to the station of perfected responsiveness.\n\nHe repeats the point, though it has already been mentioned, lest the previous discussion be taken to concern *perfected* responsiveness when it concerned responsiveness without that qualification. Then he argues that the servant's responsiveness entails a divine response to his request, using the reported words, “Uncle, if you obey Him ...” The intended sense is: my Lord hastened to answer what I desired, in recompense for my compliance with Him. This principle, in the report's terms, is not peculiar to the Prophet but applies to anyone who obeys God. Thus the servant's obedience entails that the Real responds to his request. Abū Ṭālib's “How swiftly your Lord comes to your desire” means that He responds to what you love and ask for more swiftly than to others.\n\nIn the other transmitted version, “How responsive your Lord is to you” means how promptly He answers your supplication. On the first reading, the Prophet's own rejoinder employs the rhetorical figure of *mushākala*, matching the expression of the earlier statement; on the second, Abū Ṭālib's own expression also belongs to this figure. The two versions are included because the first emphasizes the speed of response, whereas the second indicates response simply—this being the meaning intended by calling God “responsive.” The second also suggests that this way of speaking is found both before and after Islam, without being prohibited.\n\nSuch is the station of responsiveness in general. This universal will is directed toward the manifestation of every perfection capable of manifestation and toward the full realization of *jalāʾ* and *istijlāʾ*. *Jalāʾ* means the holy Essence's manifestation to itself within itself, while *istijlāʾ* means [the corresponding manifestation expounded on p. 141].",

    {
      "id": "MSH-P143",
      "pair_sequence": 1,
      "old_en": "**Al-Mahāʾimī:** [The explanation concerns] the distinction from responsiveness in general. Answering a mere act of willing is a mark of perfected responsiveness because the servant of this qualification mirrors, in his very reality, what the Real desires of him in the first universal will directed toward complete *jalāʾ* and *istijlāʾ*. Consequently, he has no will distinct from the Real's will: he mirrors his Lord's will and the other divine attributes. His will is the shadow of the divine will—indeed, under the consideration of reality, its very counterpart. He therefore does not need to supplicate, because his petition is absorbed into willing, and his willing does not stand apart from the will of his Lord. What occurs is whatever the Lord wills, since the Real effects what He wills and no intended thing fails to conform to that will. Universal existence responds to Him by nature, like the limbs of a healthy human being under his perfected faculties. A mirror lit by His light conveys the illumination to what faces it, as water lit by the sun lights up an opposing wall. Therefore **he effects what he wills through his Lord, not through himself**.\n\nQūnawī then describes one who has attained a still higher realization of *jalāʾ* and *istijlāʾ* and abides in *baqāʾ*. Such a person does not dissolve his petition into willing; rather, both his petition and his willing are answered. If he prays, he does so through the outward tongues of all worlds and through their ranks—which express implicit requests through states, receptivities, and other conditions—because he mirrors them all. Their petitions are, on this account, answered. If he does not pray, his will is answered because his omission of petition proceeds from his being a locus of manifestation of the Real. The Real does not supplicate, for supplication belongs to the servant; **God is too exalted to become a servant, just as a servant is too lowly to become a Lord**. Every restricted thing has an aspect facing unrestrictedness; in this servant that aspect is perfected because he is a complete locus of manifestation. Consequently his will mirrors the will of the One who effects what He wills.\n\n**Qūnawī:** “Beyond this station there is no further target for the aspirant, no ladder to another rank or station. Beneath it stands one who turns to the Real with complete knowledge and correct conception, the one meant by the address, ‘Call upon Me and I shall answer you.’ The Real's report is true. As that servant has succeeded in doing what has been described, the conclusion necessarily follows: he must be answered—unlike the other kinds of people turning toward Him whose states we have discussed. Know this and you will attain precious secrets and unfamiliar sciences which neither thoughts nor understandings have reached and which fingers have not inscribed with pens. God is the guide.”\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** That is, there is no object of aspiration beyond this actualization of perfect responsiveness, through which the servant becomes a mirror of [the explanation continues on p. 144].",

      "old_en": "**Al-Mahāʾimī:** [The preceding section closes:] There is no further object at which aspiration can aim beyond the actualization of the servant as a mirror, in his own reality, of what the Real desires through the first universal will relating to the perfection of *jalāʾ* and *istijlāʾ*, together with that realization in the station of *baqāʾ*.       "pair_sequence": 1,
      "old_en": "**Al-Mahāʾimī:** [The Perfect Human is a manifestation of the Real] in the way He knows Himself through Himself within Himself, and a mirror for what the Real intends by the first universal will, together with the consequences and manner of this mirroring. These are weighty matters, hence the description “a noble text.”\n\n**Qūnawī:** “Know that the highest degrees of knowledge of anything, for any knower whatever, whether the object of knowledge be one thing or many things, arise only through union with the known and the absence of otherness between the knower and it. The cause of ignorance of a thing, preventing full apprehension of it, is nothing other than the predominance of the ruling of that by which the knower and known are each distinguished from the other. This is a non-spatial distance; distance, wherever it occurs, obstructs complete apprehension of what is distant. Degrees of knowing a thing vary according to the extent to which the ruling of that by which the knower and known are united prevails. This is true nearness, which removes the separation that constitutes true remoteness, indicated by the rulings of difference and distinction.”\n\n**Al-Mahāʾimī:** The difference between this discussion and the third derivative proposition of the earlier texts is that the latter dealt with perfect encompassing of a thing and showed that such encompassing is impossible. The present discussion concerns the cause of knowledge and how it can attain the highest possible degree of apprehension.\n\nThe highest degree of knowledge is considered whether its object is the Real or creation, and whether its knower belongs to the order of the Real or of creatures. The object may be one intrinsically, like a simple thing; one accidentally, like a composite; or plural as plural. Al-Mahāʾimī schematically divides the cases into eight: the Real knowing Himself alone, Himself with the world, one creature alone, or that creature with the rest of the world; and a creature knowing the Real alone, the Real with the world, itself alone, or itself with another creature. Each case is approached through the union of knower and known and the exclusion of otherness.\n\nIn the first and seventh cases this is evident. In the others, the known must have a likeness present to the knower, with its image impressed in the mirror of knowledge so that, to vision, it is not distinguished from the mirror. **This** is what “union” signifies in the explanatory analogy.     {
      "id": "MSH-P146",
      "pair_sequence": 1,
      "old_en": "**Al-Mahāʾimī:** [Ignorance arises from the dominance of] the factor by which knower and known are distinguished from one another. This could seem to assume what requires proof, so Qūnawī describes it as non-spatial distance, which impedes knowledge. Distance—whether sensible or intellectual—prevents a complete grasp of the remote object, since not all its accidental characteristics, qualities, and measures can then be known.\n\nThe point is apparent in sensory distance. In the non-sensory case, an analogy is used—called *tamthīl* as a procedure of exposition, though a direct insight according to realization: non-sensory distance prevents the likeness of the known from being fully present in the knower, just as physical distance impairs the complete presentation of what is seen to the faculty of sight. If distance produces ignorance, nearness produces knowledge. Distance and nearness are relational, however, and their degrees are neither simply identical nor precisely measurable. Consequently, degrees of comprehensive knowing and ignorance vary with the prevalence of that aspect through which knower and known are united.\n\nQūnawī calls the ruling of the unifying factor “true nearness,” since nearness in space, time, or qualities is mediated, whereas this nearness has no intermediary. True nearness removes separation, difference, and otherness, which comprise true remoteness, whether sensory or intellectual. His initial statement could suggest that remoteness is exclusively non-sensory. The intention, however, was first to explain intellectual distance by analogy with sensible distance, then to establish the obstructive character of both. It is like the other conceptual universals: its extramental realization would require the addition either of determination or of something necessarily connected with determination. One should not object that, if this general negation obtains among other identities, contradictories would be joined; if not, it would be impossible to affirm the negation of anything besides that identity. For though the expression is differentiated according to the identities, as such it is not actual except through certain relations. These doubts have also been confronted with alleged proofs that existence is identical with quiddities. One such proof says: if existence were additional, quiddities as such would be nonexistent, so an existent would be qualified by nonexistence.",
      "new_en": "**Objection:** What is negated is only a particular identity, and the exhaustive distinction is between its being and its removal. **Reply:** Ordinary understanding takes the expression universally. One should not object that, if this general negation obtains among other identities, contradictories would be joined; if not, it would be impossible to affirm the negation of anything besides that identity. For although it is [the wording علما here is uncertain] with respect to the identities, it has no actuality simply as such, but only through certain relations. These doubts have also been confronted with alleged proofs that existence is identical with quiddities. One such proof says: if existence were additional, quiddities as such would be nonexistent, so the existent would be qualified by the nonexistent.",
      "reason": "Avoids silently translating the doubtful علما as its apparent opposite (differentiated); renders بالمعدوم as the nonexistent rather than the abstract العدم."
    },
    {
      "id": "MSH-030",
      "pair_sequence": 3,
      "old_en": "**Reply:** Quiddities considered in themselves are characterised by neither existence nor nonexistence. These are joined to them as blackness or whiteness may be joined to a body. **Another objection:** Every positive attribute of a thing presupposes that thing's own establishment. Existence would therefore need an existence prior to its own existence, producing self-priority and an infinite regress. **Reply:** That principle of presupposition applies to a positive attribute which is *other than existence*. **Another objection:** If existence were additional, it would itself require existence. **Reply:** A thing's being established as itself is not something additional to it. That nonexistence cannot befall existence is likewise self-evident; the preceding argument serves to bring this out. Nonexistence would either befall existence as an accident—in which case one contradictory would be qualified by its opposite—or else existence would turn into a different nature. Both are necessarily impossible.",
      "new_en": "**Reply:** Quiddities considered in themselves are characterised by neither existence nor nonexistence. These are joined to them as blackness or whiteness may be joined to a body. **Another objection:** Every positive attribute of a thing presupposes that thing's own establishment. Quiddities would therefore possess existence before their existence; that existence would precede itself, producing an infinite regress. **Reply:** That principle of presupposition applies to a positive attribute which is *other than existence*. **Another objection:** If existence were additional, it would itself require existence. **Reply:** A thing's being established as itself is not something additional to it. That nonexistence cannot befall existence is likewise self-evident; the preceding argument serves to bring this out. Nonexistence would either befall existence as an accident—in which case one contradictory would be qualified by its opposite—or else existence would turn into a different nature. Both are necessarily impossible.",
      "reason": "Restores the plural feminine referent لها / وجودها to the quiddities being discussed."
    },

      "id": "MSH-030",
      "pair_sequence": 4,
      "old_en": "**Objection:** The intended meaning is only that existence might cease. **Reply:** Such cessation cannot even be possible, because an impossibility cannot be possible. **Objection:** It is not impossible for one of two contradictories to qualify the other; what is impossible is to predicate the one of the other, rather than of a subject outside both which can receive either. **Reply:** [The syntax of this rebuttal is unstable in the transcription.] The impossibility of a contradictory's being predicated of itself in the proposed manner is still more evident: for example, if blackness cannot be predicated of the very subject considered as the recipient of blackness, then predicating it of blackness itself would be still more problematic. At any rate, denying that a thing can be qualified by its contradictory is mere obstinacy.",
      "new_en": "**Objection:** The intended meaning is only that existence might cease. **Reply:** Such cessation cannot even be possible, because an impossibility cannot be possible. **Objection:** It is not impossible for one of two contradictories to qualify the other; what is impossible is to predicate the one of the other, rather than of a subject outside both which can receive either. **Reply:** [The syntax of this rebuttal is unstable in the transcription.] The impossibility of a contradictory's being predicated of itself in the proposed manner is still more evident: for example, if blackness cannot be predicated of the very subject considered as the recipient of blackness, then predicating it of blackness itself would be still more problematic.     },
    {
      "id": "MSH-031",
      "pair_sequence": 1,
      "old_en": "**Objection:** Sharing entails universality, which is incompatible with real existence because a universal cannot exist outside the mind; it also entails multiple instances, which contradict divine oneness. **Reply:** What the term is predicated of is not a collection of independently existing instances. Rather the whole is one, necessary through itself, while plurality occurs through possible attributes additional to the Essence. Sharing is considered with respect to its relations to quiddities, and multiplicity with respect to its appearance within them. Thus it is not universal in the manner alleged, since all things are necessarily actual through it. Nor is it a particular marked by a merely conceptual limitation, such as being disengaged from quiddity: otherwise, when that limitation ceased to be considered, existence itself would become susceptible to nonexistence. Neither can a positive restriction qualify it: if like a form, it would render the Necessary composite; if like a differentia, it would not be a necessary concomitant of the very nature of existence. The ensuing argument about a restriction's relation to its subject is compressed and textually uncertain, but its point is to reject a distinct real delimitation that would require another principle or an infinite regress.",
      "new_en": "**Objection:** Sharing entails universality, which is incompatible with real existence because a universal cannot exist outside the mind; it also entails multiple instances, which contradict divine oneness. **Reply:** What the term is predicated of is not a collection of independently existing instances. Rather the whole is one, necessary through itself, while plurality occurs through possible attributes additional to the Essence. Sharing is considered with respect to its relations to quiddities, and multiplicity with respect to its appearance within them. Thus it is not universal in the manner alleged, since all things are necessarily actual through it. Nor is it a particular marked by a merely conceptual limitation, such as being disengaged from quiddity: otherwise, when that limitation ceased to be considered, existence itself would become susceptible to nonexistence. Neither can a positive restriction qualify it: if like a form, it would render the Necessary composite; if like a posited [restriction; the transmitted word is الفرض], it would not be a necessary concomitant of the very nature of existence. The ensuing argument about a restriction's relation to its subject is compressed and textually uncertain, but its point is to reject a distinct real delimitation that would require another principle or an infinite regress.",
